en: *The Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, Scroll One. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of Central India during the Song Dynasty. [38.6], 118–119.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One was together with immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the fourfold assembly, and immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, piśācas, bhūtas, kumbhāṇḍas, and asuras; the kings of the tānava-pūtanas, the sun and moon deities, the asuras, and various rākṣasas; the world-protectors, the four heavenly kings, Māra-deva, and others.
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded the wondrous Dharma to deliver sentient beings; it was called the *Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya of Grasping the Sword*.

It was good in the beginning, middle, and end, ultimately revealing the excellence of its meaning and flavor; it was pure throughout, fully embodying the characteristics of the stainless Brahma-conduct.

When this sutra had been spoken, not far to the north of the city of Śrāvastī, there was a village named Sana. In that village lived a poor Brahmin woman named Bhadrā, who had given birth to a son named Sarvalokābhyudgata. Having lost his father at a young age, he was now twelve years old; he was preeminent in physical beauty, strength, and the marks of a man, and he possessed brilliant eloquence, wisdom, and skill in speaking subtle words.
Furthermore, there was another village named Phalāhasi, where there lived an elder Brahmin teacher named Maṇibhadra, who was thoroughly proficient in the four Vedas.

At that time, Lokajyotirviśāla received instruction from him, serving him with humility, obedience, and reverence, and offering him his wholehearted devotion; his faculties were fully matured as he received and upheld the teachings.
Then, that teacher briefly accepted an invitation from the king and departed, leaving Lokajyotirviśāla to guard the residence.
The Brahmin’s wife was young and beautiful; upon seeing Lokajyoti, she immediately conceived a lustful mind and, suddenly forgetting the rules of propriety, reached out and grasped his garment.
At that time, Lokajyoti said to the woman:
"You are now my mother; how can you commit such an unrighteous act toward one so venerable?"
Filled with shame and trepidation, he cast off his garment and fled to a distance.
At that time, the woman’s lustful desire blazed intensely; weeping, she thought to herself:
“He has seen through me and will not comply with my wishes. If he does not follow my will, I shall surely take his life so that this man may never marry another.”

He immediately drew upon his own body with his fingernails; his lustful disorder grew ever more intense, burning him until he fell ill. He practiced the deceptions of women to adorn his person, binding himself with ropes so that his feet did not leave the ground.
At that time, Maṇibhadra, having finished his business, returned home and saw his wife hanging herself; he cut the rope with a knife and cried out in a loud voice, asking her, "Who did this?"
Then the wife replied, "This man in the world is currently practicing unrighteousness; he has forcibly oppressed me and committed such an act.
Maṇibhadra, having previously known that this man possessed great spiritual power, immediately reflected and said:

"On the day of his birth, all the swords and blades belonging to the kṣatriyas were suddenly drawn from their scabbards; the sharp blades curled up and fell to the ground, causing great terror among all the kṣatriyas."
"Since there were such extraordinary signs on the day of his birth, you should know that this man possesses great power of virtue.
Having reflected thus, he addressed the world:
"You are an evil man who has brought disgrace upon those worthy of honor; you are no longer a true Brahmin. Only by killing a thousand people can you expiate your sin."
The man, whose nature was naturally respectful and compliant, immediately addressed his teacher with words of reverence:
"Alas, Upādhyāya!
To kill a thousand people is not something I ought to do."
The teacher then said to him,
"Are you such an evil person that you do not wish to be reborn in heaven as a brāhmaṇa?
He replied:
“Preceptor! Excellent! I obey your command!
He immediately killed a thousand people and returned to pay homage at his teacher’s feet.
Having seen and heard this, the teacher felt a sense of wonder and thought:
"Is it that you, a person of such great evil, have not yet died?
He further reflected:
"Now I shall cause you to die," he said, addressing him:

"Kill one person after another, taking a finger from each; once you have killed a thousand people and taken their fingers to fashion a garland for your head, only then will you become a true Brahmin."
"For these reasons, he is named Aṅgulimāla.
He then addressed his teacher, saying:
"Excellent, Upādhyāya!"
"I shall obey!
he said, and immediately killed nine hundred and ninety-nine men.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla’s mother, thinking her son would be hungry, personally took four kinds of fine food and went to deliver it to him.
Having seen his mother, the son thought to himself,
"I must cause my mother to be reborn in the heavens.
He then immediately took up a sword, intending to go forward and take her life.
Ten yojanas less one zhang from the city of Śrāvastī, there was a tree named Aśoka.
At that time, the World-Honored One, through his omniscience, knew the proper moment and arrived like a king of geese.
When Aṅgulimāla saw the World-Honored One approaching, he grasped his sword and hurried toward him, thinking to himself:
"I shall now kill this śramaṇa Gautama once again."
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested his departure.

our minds were driven frantic by these pressing hardships, and we constantly lamented under the poison of sorrow.

At that time, seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, engaged in this profound and difficult discourse with Aṅgulimāla, and seeing that her son’s mind had been subdued, the mother extended her arms and, out of concern for her child, spoke this verse to the Buddha:
"The precious treasury lost for long is now regained; the eyes, ruined by dust and filth, are now clear and pure.
Alas, my son, his mind was deluded and distracted, constantly smearing his own body with human blood."
Holding extremely sharp swords constantly in hand, you have killed many people until they formed a heap of corpses;
you must now cause this son of yours to follow me. Now I respectfully bow my head to the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
though many people see me and revile me, and it is difficult to hear such words, your son has thus rebuked me so harshly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aṅgulimāla:
"The one beneath this tree is your mother; the debt of her life-giving kindness is profound and difficult to repay. Why do you wish to harm her so that she might be reborn in heaven?"

Aṅgulimāla! To call what is not the Dharma "the Dharma" is like the delusion of a thirsty deer chasing a springtime mirage; you are just like this, having fallen into delusion by following the instructions of an evil teacher. If sentient beings regard what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell at the end of their lives.
Aṅgulimāla! Come quickly now and take refuge in the Tathāgata. Aṅgulimāla!
Do not fear; do not be afraid.
The Great Compassion of the Tathāgata is a place of fearlessness, regarding all sentient beings as equally as Rāhula, healing all maladies and serving as a refuge for those without refuge.

The peace and security of the Tathāgata is a place of rest: he acts as a kinsman to those without kin, a treasure-store for the poor and beggars, and reveals the Unsurpassed Way to those who have lost the path to Buddhahood.
"You shall act as a protective shelter for those who are terrified and as a boat or bridge for those who are adrift and drowning.

You must swiftly cast aside your sharp sword, leave the household life to study the Way, prostrate at your mother’s feet to repent and cleanse yourself, and with utmost sincerity entreat her to grant you permission to renounce the world, so that you may deliver your mother from the suffering of the three realms of existence."

"Now you have paid the tax; you have gone forth and attained full ordination. You shall now drink the nectar-water of the Dharma. Having long wandered through the evil realms, deluded and exhausted, you shall now find rest."

"You are a tax collector, and I too am a tax collector; as a king who guards the path, I constantly receive taxes from all sentient beings, enabling them to cross over the ocean of existence in birth and death."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla immediately cast away his sword, just as a one-year-old infant lets go of fire upon grasping it; he shook his hands and wept.
Then, Aṅgulimāla’s casting away of the garland, shaking of his hands, and raising his voice in a cry were likewise just so.
Just as when a person is fast asleep and a snake suddenly bites their foot, they immediately startle awake, shake their hand, and fling it far away;
so too did Aṅgulimāla swiftly cast off his garland of fingers.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla was as if released from the possession of a non-human spirit; he became self-aware and filled with shame, blood flowing from his entire body and tears falling like rain.

Just as if a person were bitten by a snake and a skilled physician used a mantra to cause them to crawl like a serpent, so too did Aṅgulimāla writhe and crawl on his belly for thirty-nine revolutions.
Then, stepping forward, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and spoke these verses:
“How marvelous! The Perfectly Awakened One, supreme in compassion, The Teacher and Guide of Men, has come for my sake.
He enables me to cross the ocean of ignorance, With its waves of delusion and the darkness of folly.”
How marvelous is the unsurpassed compassion of the Perfectly Awakened One! The Teacher, the Charioteer of Men, has come for my sake;
he delivers me from the hardships of the wilderness of birth and death, and from the thorny forest of manifold afflictions.
How marvelous! The Perfectly Awakened One, the Supreme Joy, the Tamer and Teacher of Men, has come for my sake;
he enables me to cross over all delusions and the perils of false views, like tigers, wolves, and wild beasts.
How marvelous! The Perfectly Awakened One’s supreme equanimity— The Teacher, the Charioteer of Men, has come for my sake;
He enables me to cross over the Avīci Hell, Forever leaving behind the blazing, immeasurable suffering.
For those without a protector, you act as a protector; for those without kin, you act as a kinsman.
Having accumulated a multitude of evil karmas and heading toward great suffering, you have now come to be my refuge.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aṅgulimāla:
"Arise now and go quickly to your mother; with the utmost sincerity, repent of your transgressions and request permission to leave the household life."

At that time, Aṅgulimāla rose from the Buddha’s feet and went to his mother’s place. He circumambulated her many times, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and with sincere repentance and deep sorrow, cried out loudly.
He then addressed his mother in verse: “Alas, O compassionate mother, I have committed great transgressions; I accumulated various evil karmas, forming a mass of sin.
Following the instructions of an evil teacher, I practiced violence and harm; I killed one thousand people, lacking only one.”
Today I take refuge in my mother, and likewise take refuge in the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
today I prostrate at my mother’s feet, praying only that she will compassionately grant me permission to leave the household life.
At that time, his mother replied with a verse:
"I have now granted your permission to leave the household life for the sake of future lives;
I too shall seek the Tathāgata, to leave the household life and receive full ordination."
How marvelous and inconceivable! The Tathāgata is beyond all comparison.
Now the Buddha delivers my son, universally compassionating all the worlds.
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body possesses virtues without peer.
"I now offer this brief praise to the most supreme among gods and men.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Excellent, virtuous woman! You shall attain uninterrupted bliss."
"Now you may permit your son to go forth in my presence.
You are now old and decrepit; the time for going forth has already passed.
You should simply maintain deep faith and joy, finding rest for yourself through the Dharma."
"Wait here for a moment; King Prasenajit is arriving.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, leading the assembly of devas and his retinue of celestial maidens, emitted a bodily radiance that illuminated the city of Śrāvastī. Seeing Aṅgulimāla confronting the Buddha, his strength exhausted and his mind transformed as he was subdued and brought to repentance, he gave rise to great joy and spoke this verse:
"How marvelous is the Hero of Ten Powers, The Tamer of Men, peerless and unequaled!
He subdued Aṅgulimāla, who was constantly smeared with blood;
Dānendrarāja, the asuras, rākṣasas, fierce yakṣas and ghosts, and all other evil persons.
The nāgas and kiṃnaras, the mighty garuḍas—
upon hearing of Aṅgulimāla, they were all struck with terror and closed their eyes;
how much more so for a king among men, who would not be terrified upon seeing him?
When he was first born, the nāgas and devas were all struck with trembling fear;
all the kṣatriyas had their armor loosened and their swords and blades fallen from their hands—
how much more so for a king among men, who would not be terrified upon seeing him?
Such fierce and evil karma, the Tathāgata has completely subdued;
the Buddha’s power is inconceivable, and the realm of his wisdom is likewise so.
How marvelous is Aṅgulimāla!
Well-established in untainted precepts, my holy life is utterly pure, like a mountain of pure gold.
How marvelous! Today I have swiftly attained the benefit of the sublime Dharma!
I now offer this garment to Aṅgulimāla;
I pray that you will accept it out of compassion for me. World-Honored One, out of pity, please now bestow this upon Aṅgulimāla, so that the śramaṇa may possess robes in accordance with the Dharma.
"This great King of Beggars, the World-Honored One, observes well.
At that time, Śakra addressed Aṅgulimāla, saying:
"I pray only that you, Great Being!"
"Accept this celestial robe as your Dharma garment.
Then, Aṅgulimāla said to Śakra:
"What kind of mosquito or insignificant insect are you!"
"How could I ever accept a gift from one who lacks faith?
You are but a donkey of greed!
Having not yet crossed the long stream of the manifold sufferings of birth and death, how can you, with your naturally frail form, offer me clothing?"
"You should know that you are naturally weak in body; how could you bestow upon others a priceless robe?
It is like a king who has a thousand strongmen, yet falls to the ground even before seeing the enemy; how could he fight against the thousand strongmen of a great king of a hostile nation?"
"If I were to accept this priceless robe, how could I subdue the billions of affliction-māras and the māra of self-nature?
I shall sever immeasurable afflictions as praised by the Buddha; I must study the twelve dhūta practices of the śramaṇa. You are not a celestial king, but no different from one born blind."
"You, Śakra Devendra!
You do not understand the distinctions. What is called a violent and evil karma?
You are but a mosquito; how could you possibly know that I am a violent and wicked man?"
Alas, Śakra!
You know that Aṅgulimāla is a fierce and evil man, yet you also understand the true meaning of the Buddha-dharma; why would such a śramaṇa, having first gone forth, wear robes of priceless value?
"You are entirely ignorant of the pure dharma of renunciation. Alas, Śakra!

You are an outsider to the True Dharma of the Tathāgata. The Elder Kāśyapa, the eldest son of the Tathāgata, has abandoned eighty thousand treasuries of *maṇi* jewels and other precious stores, as well as countless other treasures and various kinds of priceless jeweled robes—discarding them like spittle—to renounce the world, study the Path, and practice the dharma of a śramaṇa, undertaking the twelve ascetic practices (*dhūta*). For what reason do you not practice with these priceless robes, but instead remain in negligence?"

The Elder Kāśyapa renounced various kinds of sweet and delicious foods and abandoned the taste of meat; he undertook and practiced the dharma of abstaining from eating meat. Begging for alms from house to house, he harbored no thoughts of aversion toward those who were unpleasant. From beginning to end, he remained consistently the same, unchanged by pleasure or pain. In the places where he begged, there were various people—some said he was nothing, while others reviled and insulted him—and he would reply: "May you be at peace."
"Then, having departed, his mind remains unshaken.
If someone says it exists, he does not give rise to greed or joy.
He replied:
“May you be at peace.
Having accepted it, he departed with his mind unshaken.

If one were to bestow great wealth upon the Saṅgha, that wealth would be used by the Saṅgha in future ages, and each of its treasuries would never be exhausted. For what reason, then, do you not offer such gifts to the Saṅgha?
Furthermore, he personally distributes [alms] to hungry ghosts, the poor, the solitary, and beggars. O Śakra!
The dharma of a śramaṇa is not to accumulate much; even salt and oil are not to be accepted or stored—this is the dharma of a śramaṇa.
To buy or sell impure things such as slaves, servants, fields, or houses is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it is the dharma of a householder.
Whether giving or receiving such impure things, it is all likewise so.
"You mass of great ignorance!

Beings such as these must now be subdued, just as one treats tares and weeds that harm good seedlings. Those whom I have killed to make my finger-garland were all beings who destroy the Dharma; not a single one among them was a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā."
At that time, Śakra said to Aṅgulimāla:
"The characteristic of non-harming is itself the Dharma; the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings equally as he does Rāhula. How, then, can you permit the subduing of wicked people?"
Aṅgulimāla said:
"How do you know the distinction between harming and not harming?
It is like the skillful means of a conjurer, which others do not understand."
Since such Bodhisattvas understand the realm of illusion, how can you, who stand outside the Buddha-dharma, know that both harm and non-harm each have two kinds?
There is the non-harm of Śrāvakas, and there is the non-harm of Bodhisattvas.
"You, a mere mosquito, how could you know the two kinds of non-harming?
The difference between your sphere and the sphere of a bodhisattva is like a mosquito's wing covering the sky."
"For example, if a śramaṇa were possessed by a non-human spirit, at that time, should the great assembly protect him?
Śakra replied, "They should indeed protect him."
He asked, "If death results from such protection,
who should be held guilty? Śakra replied:
"To purify and eliminate a harmful mind, there is no offense for one who does not commit a transgression. Aṅgulimāla said:
"In this way, when taming various evil elephants, if one should cause them to die, the person who guards [the herd] commits no offense and shall obtain immeasurable, supreme merit."
In this way, the distinction between harming and non-harming is difficult to discern; this is called the bodhisattva’s non-harming. He asked:
“Suppose, for example, a skilled physician treats a patient by using a hook to pull out his tongue; if the patient were to die as a result, would the physician be guilty of a transgression?”
He replied, "No.
That skilled physician was of great benefit to many; he was free from any harmful intent."
He asked, "If one were to cause the death of such beings who resemble tameless elephants in order to subdue them, would that be considered a transgression?
He replied:
"No. One shall obtain immeasurable and sublime merit, provided that one excludes any harmful intent. He asked:
“Suppose, for example, a disciple receives instruction from a teacher and dies as a result of that teaching;
would the teacher be guilty? He replied, “No.”
"Except when there is a harmful intent. He asked:
"If a being of such majestic power and radiant clarity were to cause a beast as wicked as an elephant to die upon seeing him, would there be an offense of concealment?"
He replied, "No,
except when there is a harmful intent."
"Therefore, Śakra! You do not understand the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome karma;

you do not understand the distinction between those who are śramaṇas and those who are not. Those who resemble evil elephants and destroy the True Dharma should be subdued—just as the eighty great śrāvakas, beginning with the Elder Kāśyapa and including Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, all abandoned vast treasuries of great jewels to leave the household life and study the Path. Within the True Dharma, they were content with few desires. Why, then, should a bhikṣu practice the wearing of priceless robes?"
All these have shaved their heads and removed arrogance; they wander alone, carrying alms bowls to beg for food to sustain their lives and wearing dyed robes. How could such bhikṣus be negligent?

Constantly oppressed by cold and heat, hunger and thirst, his feet tread upon dust and soil like those of a wild deer; he does not transgress even the smallest precept, as a yak cherishes its tail, guarding them without forsaking them as a crow broods over its chicks; like an elephant with broken tusks, he no longer possesses outward beauty—what need would he have for the practice of priceless garments?

You who stand outside the True Dharma, be careful not to speak further; like those heretics and outcasts (*caṇḍāla*), you shall ultimately never enter the assembly of the twice-born. You are likewise an outcast outside the True Dharma; you, a mere mosquito, remain silent and make no sound!
The Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra, Scroll One;
The Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
At that time, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, emitted a great radiance that illuminated the city of Śrāvastī.
With single-minded devotion, he joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and having made offerings to the Tathāgata and Aṅgulimāla, he spoke these verses:
"How marvelous! Today I behold a great battle, Like two fierce and powerful lions contending."
How marvelous! The Tamer, Teacher of Gods and Men, The Tathāgata has skillfully tamed Aṅgulimāla.

Just as a venomous snake, upon seeing a master of mantras, Huffs its breath and releases poison without fear, Yet the master immediately subdues it and brings it to stillness— So too is the Great Master of the Three Realms.
Having subdued the fierce Aṅgulimāla, I now bow my head to the Physician of the Three Worlds;
with inconceivable and great supernormal powers, I now bow my head to the Sovereign King.
The establishment by Mahādeva is most extraordinary; by means of the Dharma, he established Aṅgulimāla.
His deeds are supreme and beyond comparison; therefore, he is named the Peerless Honored One.
Aṅgulimāla now performs supreme deeds; abiding in the precepts, he is tamed and utterly tranquil.
With body and mind secure and free from fear, he is like the naturally pure golden hue, as refined and exquisite as Jambūnada gold.
May Aṅgulimāla be clothed in celestial robes, and may I thereby attain great bodhi;
as he wears these robes and guards his holy life, may his mind remain ultimately pure and unshakable.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla said to the Brahmā King:
"Who are you, speaking so much and using double-tongued speech, saying:
'Aṅgulimāla has associated with my robes and long practiced the holy life'?"
Yet you were seen to be reviled and insulted: "You are a wicked Brahmā, not a true Brahmā, though bearing the likeness of one.
You are like a mosquito that has come and said, 'I am Brahmā.'"
"What is the meaning of 'brahman'?
What is meant by 'worldly brahmanic practice'?
Would I ever don the garments of mosquitoes and gnats to cultivate the holy life?"

I am not a hired laborer, nor can I act according to another's will; I am not a person in debt. I am like a *śirīṣaka*—a foreign conjurer who performs the feat of flying, moving back and forth through the air with extreme speed, going quickly and returning quickly.

You, a mere mosquito, are just like this: having gone to experience the bliss of Brahmā, you have returned to fall here. You do not know the true merit of a Bodhisattva’s taking birth; you mistake what is not the Dharma for the Dharma. Like those of your kind, you fail to perceive the cycle of birth and death and remain deluded in its turning.
Alas, Brahmā!
Do you truly know good and evil?
You say that Aṅgulimāla has committed great evil deeds; what do you, a wretched Brahmā who is like a mosquito or a gnat, know of this?
"You should train yourself in the conduct of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Brahma King replied to Aṅgulimāla, saying:
"You have already killed nine hundred and ninety-nine people; even now, you are seen to be violent and unrestrained, such that even the eagles and vultures do not dare to approach you."
This is not a person of violent arrogance; where else could there be one truly arrogant?
This is not an evil Māra; where else could there be a true Māra?
"Aṅgulimāla! Do not be negligent;
employ skillful means to eliminate the evil karma you have created.
Excellent, O Tathāgata!"
"Truly, you possess great compassion, for you are able to deliver such fierce and violent beings as Aṅgulimāla.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla said to the Brahmā King:
"Evil Brahmā, you who are like a mosquito—where will you go?"
Furthermore, where would you go astray?
Not knowing the difference between good and evil, sentient beings die and fall into the evil realms.
It is like a person who, traveling through a thicket at night, sees fireflies atop a tree and returns in terror, saying to the people in the city:
“The forest is on fire!
At that time, a great multitude of people went together to see it; seeing that it was merely fireflies, they knew it was not the forest burning.
Now you, O wicked Brahmā, are just like this, proclaiming:
"I am deluded," he says, deceiving himself and deceiving others; you and the others shall later realize for yourselves that this is a mere accumulation of illusions.
It is like a foolish man who, having entered a thicket and seen the flowers of an *aśoka* tree, calls them fire; terrified, he returns home and enters the city to tell the people:
"That forest has been burned.
When the people went to see it, they realized it was not actually fire.

You, a mere mosquito, are just like this: you and others shall later know for yourselves what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, and you shall also know for yourselves that this is but a phantom accumulation. Do not speak such false words again; you should remain silent and not practice lying.
At that time, the Four World-Protecting Kings came to where the Buddha was, making great offerings to the Buddha and Aṅgulimāla.
Having made these offerings, they addressed the Tathāgata and Aṅgulimāla, speaking in verse:
"How marvelous! How truly rare!"
The Hero of the World now engages in a great battle, answering questions on the primary truth; the light of wisdom dispels the darkness of delusion.
How marvelous is the Well-Tamed One, the unsurpassed Teacher of gods and men!
Therefore, possessing immeasurable power, he is titled the Tathāgata.
The foremost Padma, with feet pure and supple, unstained by dust or water; therefore, I bow my head in homage.
Now I take refuge in the Buddha and with single-minded devotion entreat that my wishes be fulfilled.
Let Aṅgulimāla now enjoy our alms-bowl.
Aṅgulimāla is now as beautiful as the moon in the sky;
Aṅgulimāla is adorned with the perfect radiance of pure precepts.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla said to the Four Great Kings:
"Who are you, mere mosquitoes and small insects?
You who protect the world, protect the world, yet are so arrogant as to proclaim: "
"I shall give you a celestial alms-bowl," he said, yet I was treated with contempt and insult.
Wait a moment and watch my difficulty; in a short while you shall see me holding an earthenware vessel—what use is such a negligent bowl as this?

Yet they boastfully claim the title of "World Protector" (Lokapāla); those called World Protectors are so named because they are able to subdue various evil beings such as wild elephants, rather than because they protect the world by guarding the true Dharma. They are merely termed World Protectors [in that limited sense].
For example, suppose there is a person who hears the cry of a cuckoo and sees its form, but then upon seeing a crow, they become confused and say: "Cuckoo, cuckoo!"
"You all act in this way, taking what is not Dharma to be Dharma and protecting what is not Dharma, just like those who saw a crow and thought it was a cuckoo.
You should protect the Dharma; do not protect the world."
"O mosquitoes and gadflies, and you four kings, each remain silent!
At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyas approached the Buddha; having made offerings to the Buddha, he withdrew to stand to one side and addressed Aṅgulimāla with these verses:
"You should now quickly leave the household life, For you have come to deceive me and enter my city."
"I do not even think of you; I shall simply cause you to emerge from hell.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
"Go far away, you thief-dog, you fearless mosquito who speaks!"
And while you have not yet been bound by the five fetters, Pāpīyān, you should depart quickly;
do not let me, for even a moment, kick a wretched dog with my left foot.
When [the world] is empty and devoid of self, you may roam the palaces as you please.
Like the King of Golden-Winged Birds, dwelling upon the summit of Mount Sumeru,
he looks down into the great ocean where the various dragons sport together.
The Bodhisattva, the King of Golden-Winged Birds, sports above the hells.
Quickly drink the water of liberation, looking down upon sentient beings in suffering.
The thief-dog Mara remains silent; listen attentively to the Dharma of ambrosia, and thereafter return to the heavens, indulging in all your desires as you wish.
At that time, the deity Maheśvara, having made a great offering for the Tathāgata and Aṅgulimāla, withdrew to stand to one side. With joy and reverence meeting within him, he praised them in verse:
"I now pay homage at the feet of the Honored One; With joy and reverence, I speak this gāthā:
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body Is like the utpala lotus."
With teeth as white as the kumuda lily, eyes as pure as the thousand-petaled lotus,
wisdom untainted and purity surpassing the puṇḍarīka—
how marvelous is Aṅgulimāla!
"Though dwelling on the stage of an ordinary person, you are able to subdue Māra;
you shall swiftly attain perfect enlightenment and universally save all worlds.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
“Who are you, of such a lowly station,
falsely claiming to be Maheśvara and assuming the name ‘The Sovereign,’ yet not being a true Sovereign King?
How can you now know that I abide on the level of an ordinary person?”
Long-toothed Piśāca, you should quickly answer what is asked.
Though your form is as hideous as that of a leper,
you extensively preach the methods for treating leprosy to all the world.
If you cannot save yourself from your own illness, how can you cure the diseases of others?
Now you, a mere mosquito, are likewise deluded by ignorance;
not knowing your own nature and destiny, how can you know the minds of others?
Yet you speak of Aṅgulimāla as dwelling on the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
You should not anoint him as a sovereign king in his stead;
being ignorant, remain silent for a moment, and you shall see for yourself in an instant.
At that time, there was a deity dwelling in the tree upon which the Tathāgata sat. Seeing Aṅgulimāla, the deity conceived a heart of reverence and faith, and praised him in verse:
"Come quickly, Aṅgulimāla! Heroic one of firm wisdom, I now invite you to don the dharma robes; I offer you this first meal."
"By giving to you and to the Tathāgata, you shall attain the foremost fruit.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
"The Tathāgata has never eaten, and the Śrāvakas are likewise so."
"To whom do you now intend to give?
Speak quickly to resolve our doubt.
At that time, the tree deity addressed him with these verses:
"The Tathāgata always partakes of food, and the śrāvakas do likewise;
those who are firm in their desire to leave the household life should not utter false speech.
They should abandon hypocrisy, for crookedness is not pure."
"If a person transgresses even one dharma, that is itself false speech;
they will not cross over to the next world, and there is no evil they will not commit.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
“You are of low birth; what do you wish to say now?
Observe this for yourself: women are censured by the Buddha;
who in the world speaks falsely?”
Who speaks the truth?
Who in the world craves food?
Who in the world suffers from birth and death?
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the true merits of the Great Self (mahātman), yet sentient beings are unable to know this; this would indeed be a falsehood.
To say one has eaten when one has not eaten—this would indeed be a falsehood.
Since he does not even have the going forth, how much less could he receive full ordination?
Not knowing that it was spoken with intentional concealment, this constitutes a false speech.
Since he does not even have the going forth, how much less could he receive full ordination?
"I have not transgressed a single dharma, whereas you have transgressed immeasurable ones.
Quickly go before the God among Gods and repent to eliminate your false speech.
At that time, the tree deity challenged him with these verses:
“For what reason do you say that I am of low birth?
Without having abandoned the state of a piśāca, how could one know male or female?
At that time, Aṅgulimāla replied in verse:
"Just as when a Universal Monarch’s throne, adorned with rare jewels,
is briefly occupied by a foul-smelling dog, which then returns to its place of impurity;
so too do you, with your base and inferior nature, briefly wander through the skillful methods."
Return once more to the body of a maiden, and let your mind indulge in the pleasures of the five desires.
You should now employ skillful means to quickly cast off this female dog’s body;
do not grasp at the marks of male or female, but practice the dharma of emptiness and stillness.
"Having cultivated the dharma of emptiness, one will swiftly attain the male nature.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, like kings of geese, arrived through the air by means of their supernormal powers. Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side; seeing Aṅgulimāla, they felt sympathetic joy in their hearts.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana praised him in verse:
"O heroic man of wisdom, you who have excellently cultivated such sublime deeds!
You should quickly follow the Buddha, leave the household life, and practice the pure precepts."
Together with fellow practitioners of the holy life, we have traveled through the air to the Jeta Grove.
We pray that the Buddha will compassionately grant us permission to leave the household life and receive full ordination,
so that all throughout the world may together look up to us in reverence.
Soaring through space like the king of geese, Radiant and pure as the full moon.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla asked in verse:
“What are the supernatural powers of the world?”
"What is the basis of supernormal powers?
Who is the foremost in spiritual might? Speak quickly to sever my doubts.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied in verse:
"If a person cultivates pure equanimity, constantly bestows sandals and vehicles,
and a bhikṣu maintains pure precepts while remaining far removed from and not associating with [the unwholesome],
through these two causes and conditions, they will swiftly attain supernormal powers."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke again in verse:
"Alas, Mahāmaudgalyāyana! You practice the conduct of a mosquito;
You are unable to discern or know The foremost, true supernormal power."
When mosquitoes and gnats come upon one from the void, it is fitting to remain silent out of ignorance.
Constantly practicing for the benefit of oneself and others, may I swiftly bring peace to all sentient beings;
by cultivating such skillful means, one quickly attains the supreme supernormal powers.
To comfort those who preach the Dharma, And whenever they encounter suffering and hardship,
I shall sacrifice my own body to protect them, So that they may swiftly attain the supreme supernormal powers.
I shall now proceed with speed To extensively deliver all living beings.
Upon reaching the Jeta Grove, one shall attain great supernormal powers.
Such is the immeasurable, namely the Mahāyāna;
it is limitless and boundless, namely the state of all Tathāgatas.
At that time, after Aṅgulimāla had spoken these verses, he again spoke in verse,
questioning Śāriputra: “O Śāriputra, how is it that the great wisdom of the world—
whence does this wisdom arise?”
"Speak quickly to resolve our doubts.
At that time, Śāriputra replied in verse:
"By skillfully upholding the five precepts, One is able to achieve great wisdom."
"When life ends and one receives another body, wisdom is always born together [with it];
fame spreads far and wide, and wisdom remains unshakable.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke again in verse:
“The Buddha taught that which is eternal and imperishable; from this, great wisdom arises.
The Buddha taught great wisdom; from this, the teaching of the Dharma arises.
Alas, Śāriputra! You have practiced the conduct of a mosquito.”
Unable to discern the meaning of true wisdom, the intellect of mosquitoes is indeed base; being ignorant, you should remain silent.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Seeing Aṅgulimāla, his heart was filled with sympathetic joy, and he praised him in verse, saying:
“Excellent, Aṅgulimāla!
Having already cultivated such sublime deeds, I now express my sympathetic joy; may you swiftly master the ninefold scriptures.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla addressed him with a verse, saying:
“The Tathāgata has praised you as the foremost among those of great learning.
What constitutes ‘great learning’ in the world, and from what does such great learning arise?
At that time, Ānanda replied in verse:
"By reciting and studying the ninefold canon, and by teaching it to others free from stinginess,
one thereby attains great learning and inconceivable dhāraṇī.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke again in verse:
"Praising all the Tathāgatas as being ultimately and eternally imperishable—this is called being the foremost and most learned in the world.
Alas, Ānanda! You have practiced the conduct of a mosquito."
"Unable to discern or know, yet claiming to have entered the hearing of the learned—how base is the grasp of a mosquito! Being ignorant, you should remain silent.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Seeing Aṅgulimāla, his heart felt sympathetic joy, and he praised him with these verses:
“Excellent, Aṅgulimāla!
You have already cultivated supreme merit; I now express my sympathetic joy and reverently and swiftly uphold your precepts.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla asked in verse:
“The Tathāgata has praised you as foremost in revering the precepts.
How does one revere the pure precepts for the sake of the world?
You are the Buddha’s beloved son; speak quickly and resolve my doubt.”
At that time, Rāhula replied in verse:
"Whatever has been spoken by all the Buddhas, To uphold it with single-minded reverence—
This is the foremost precept of reverence In this world."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke again in verse:
“If one speaks of all Tathāgatas as the foremost permanence in the world,
this is called the supreme precept of veneration in the world.”
Alas, Rāhula! You cannot know the foremost, true respect for the precepts;
how base is the reverence of a mosquito! Being ignorant, you should remain silent.

At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Seeing Aṅgulimāla, his heart was filled with sympathetic joy, and he praised him in verse, saying:
“How marvelous, Aṅgulimāla!
"Having well cultivated sublime deeds, I now express my sympathetic joy; before long, you shall attain the divine eye.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla asked in verse:
"The Tathāgata has praised you, saying that your divine eye is the foremost."
"What is the celestial eye of the world? How does the celestial eye arise?
You should now speak quickly to resolve the doubts I have.
At that time, Aniruddha replied in verse:
"Always delighting in giving lamps, preaching the Dharma to enlighten and transform others,
by this one obtains the divine eye, seeing through all things without obstruction.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke again in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s profound treasury of Dharma, Expounded through diligent skillful means, Revealed without concealment— The ultimate, most supreme eye.
Alas, Aniruddha! You have practiced the conduct of a mosquito.”
Unable to know the birth [of beings], nor the supreme skillful means of the divine eye—how wretched is the eye of a mosquito! Being ignorant, you should remain silent.

At that time, the Venerable Śramaṇa Droṇa approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Seeing Aṅgulimāla, his heart felt sympathetic joy, and he praised him in verse, saying:
"How marvelous, Aṅgulimāla!
You have skillfully cultivated such sublime deeds; I now express my sympathetic joy (anumodana) and exhort you: 'You should cultivate patience.
" At that time, Aṅgulimāla asked in verse:
"How does one become a person of the world who achieves the foremost patience?
How does one give rise to forbearance?
Speak quickly to resolve our doubts."
At that time, the śramaṇa Dāsa replied in verse:
“Though sandalwood is smeared upon my right arm, And a sharp blade cuts off my left hand, My mind remains equanimous and unshaken;
Thus I am able to give rise to the highest patience.”
"This is what is called the world, the supreme subduer of the Enduring One.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke again in verse:
"If one speaks of the Tathāgatagarbha, it reveals all worlds."
Those who are ignorant, evil, and hold wrong views,
yet say that "abandoning me" means "there is no self" is the Buddha’s true Dharma— when they hear such a teaching,
they are not afraid. Free from pride, they sacrifice their bodies and lives to extensively proclaim the Tathāgatagarbha.
This is called the world; it is the supreme subduer of the patient one (*kṣānti*).
Alas, O Śramaṇa!
You practice the conduct of a mosquito, yet you cannot know the arising of the most supreme skillful means of patience (*kṣānti-upāya*).
"Even mosquitoes can endure the sufferings of hunger, thirst, cold, and heat;
yet how wretched is the endurance of a mosquito! Being ignorant, it is right for it to remain silent.

At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Seeing Aṅgulimāla, his heart was filled with great joy, and he praised him in verse, saying:
“Excellent is the cultivation of sublime deeds; I now express my sympathetic joy.
For the sake of all sentient beings, you comfort them by expounding the Dharma.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla asked in verse:
“The Tathāgata has praised you as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
How does one preach the Dharma?
How does one understand its meaning?”
"I only pray that the Supreme Dharma-Teacher will, at this time, resolve my doubts.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied in verse:
"That which neither the Buddhas nor the śrāvakas, nor even the noble ones, have attained as a dharma—"
The Perfectly Awakened One has thoroughly realized this and extensively expounded it for the sake of sentient beings. What is the meaning of this teaching?

It means that all Buddhas of the past sought with the utmost skillful means among all phenomena, yet they did not find a realm of sentient beings, nor a self, a person, or a life-span. All Buddhas of the present and future, as well as all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the three periods of time, likewise sought with the utmost skillful means among all phenomena and found nothing at all. I also teach sentient beings in this same way: apart from a realm of sentient beings, a self, a person, or a life-span, I teach the Dharma of non-self and the Dharma of emptiness; such is the teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla said to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"Alas, Pūrṇa! You practice the conduct of a mosquito yet do not know how to preach the Dharma."

Alas! The ignorant mosquitoes remain silent, unaware of the Tathāgata’s teaching of intentional concealment; they claim that there is no self in phenomena, falling into the lamp of folly like moths rushing into a flame.

That which all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot find refers to this: all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, sought with the utmost skillful means within all sentient beings and could not find the absence of the *tathāgatagarbha*;
all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the present, seek with the utmost skillful means within all sentient beings and cannot find the absence of self-nature (*anātmatā*);
all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the future, will seek with the utmost skillful means within all sentient beings and will not find the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Throughout the three periods of time, all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, despite employing every possible skillful means among all sentient beings to seek the Tathāgatagarbha, cannot find it.
This is the true meaning of the Tathāgata’s verse.

"Furthermore, that which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not find refers to the fact that all past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, sought the 'self' of the world among all phenomena through every possible skillful means—whether it be the size of a thumb, a grain of rice, sesame, wheat, or mustard seed; or whether it be blue, yellow, red, white, square, round, long, or short—and yet found no such various characteristics."
Some say: "It is in the heart, or above or below the navel. Others say:
"Head, eyes, and all parts of the body," or it is said:
"Throughout the entire body, they are like perspiration."
"Thus, with such immeasurable and manifold deluded conceptions, you cultivate a self according to worldly conventions and likewise say:
'It is eternally abiding, blissful, and at rest.

Yet, when compared to me, all Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas have not attained the perfect awakening to that dharma to preach it for the sake of sentient beings. This is the true meaning of the Tathāgata’s verse; it is not as you have just explained through your deluded conceptions."

"Furthermore, that which all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, cannot obtain is as follows: All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, sought the Tathāgata-garbha through the utmost skillful means and found it unobtainable; the nature of the Tathāgata is non-action, yet within all sentient beings it is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs.

All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the present, seek the Tathāgata-garbha through the utmost skillful means and find it unobtainable; the nature of the Tathāgata is non-action, yet within all sentient beings it is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs.

All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the future, will seek the Tathāgata-garbha through the utmost skillful means and find it unobtainable; this non-action is the nature of the Tathāgata, yet within all sentient beings it is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs."
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of the three periods of time possess the Tathāgatagarbha, yet they do not see it with their eyes; one should explain the causes and conditions for this.

It is like Rāhula, who, out of his profound reverence for the precepts, looked most intently at pure water but could not discern whether there were insects—whether they were insects, or not insects, or perhaps fine dust.
By observing closely for a long time, one gradually perceives subtle insects. It is the same with a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages:

while observing the self-nature within his own body, he gives rise to various different views regarding immeasurable natures. The Tathāgata-garbha is thus difficult to enter; it is likewise extremely difficult for one to provide comforting explanations of it. This refers to those who, during the most fiercely burning times of a degenerate age, do not spare their own bodies or lives to preach the Tathāgata-garbha for the sake of sentient beings. For this reason, I say that the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, the heroes among men, are themselves the Tathāgatas.

For example, Aniruddha, who is foremost in the divine eye, can clearly and truly see the tracks of birds in the sky; yet when he travels together with those possessing only the fleshly eye, those with fleshly eyes cannot see them. They must rely on faith in Aniruddha to know that bird-tracks exist. In the same way, how can the foolish fleshly-eyed Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas perceive the nature of the Buddha-realm, which exists within the *tathāgatagarbha* as taught in the Buddhist scriptures? They can only do so by relying on faith.
"If even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas still rely on the faith of others, how can ordinary beings who are born blind know for themselves without receiving it from another?

'I have heard that former Buddhas spoke of this land: at the beginning of the kalpa there were four kinds of flavors; the sentient beings of that time who ate those four flavors now eat earth, and because of long-standing habituation, they still do not abandon it.'"

Those who have cultivated the Tathāgatagarbha under various Tathāgatas of the past are likewise so; because they have practiced it for a long time, even now they continue to believe in and delight in it, practicing throughout the long night to repay the kindness of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, in the future, those who hear of the Tathāgatagarbha from a teacher of the Dharma and, having heard it, believe and rejoice in it—unlike other sentient beings who are like those eating earth—they, being those who believe and rejoice, are children of the Tathāgata repaying the kindness of the Tathāgata.

For example, the *kukkuta* bird has been devoid of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*) since time immemorial and fails to repay the kindness of its nurturer; because of this long-standing habituation, it does not abandon these traits even now.

Those sentient beings are just like this: in past lives they were devoid of shame and remorse; having been devoid of them, they are devoid of them now, and they will remain devoid of them in the future. Upon hearing of the *tathāgatagarbha*, they do not give rise to faith or joy; having lacked such faith and joy, they lack it now, and they will lack it in the future.

For example, the monkey’s form is extremely ugly and hideous; it is constantly filled with alarm and fear, its mind as restless and agitated as surging waves upon water, which does not yet cease even now due to the force of past habituation.

Those sentient beings are also like this: their minds, throughout the past, future, and present, are always fickle and restless; hearing of the Tathāgatagarbha, they do not give rise to faith or joy, just as an owl is blind by day and sees at night, preferring darkness and loathing light.

Those sentient beings are also like this: they prefer what is false and evil while disliking what is correct, and they take no pleasure in seeing the Buddha or the Tathāgatagarbha; they do not give rise to faith or joy regarding the past, future, or present, just as that owl prefers darkness and dislikes light.

Just as a person who has practiced wrong views throughout the long night and become stained by the improper doctrines of various non-Buddhist paths does not yet abandon them even now due to the force of past habituation, so too it is with those sentient beings.

Having long practiced the teachings that conceal the absence of self, like those common fools stained by various heterodox doctrines, they do not understand the esoteric teachings of the past, future, or present; they will not give rise to faith or joy regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*, whereas other sentient beings might.

If there are people who, in the past, encountered various Buddhas, made offerings, served them, and heard of the Tathāgatagarbha—even if they were able to hear and receive it for only the duration of a finger-snap—due to these roots of goodness their faculties have become fully matured; thus, wherever they are born, they possess excellence, nobility, and mastery. These sentient beings remain so matured even now, being born with excellence, nobility, and mastery.

Because they encountered various Buddhas in the past and were able to hear of the Tathāgatagarbha for a time, in future lives, upon hearing of the Tathāgatagarbha again, they shall believe and rejoice in it, practicing according to the teaching. Their faculties will be fully matured; they will possess wealth, nobility, and mastery, with physical strength and vigor complete and wisdom clear and penetrating. Their Brahma-voice will be pure, such that all will love and delight in it. They may become a Cakravartin King, or a prince, or a great minister. Endowed with virtuous qualities, they will be free from pride and self-indulgence; they will subdue sleep, practice with diligence, and be free from negligence, as well as achieving all other meritorious virtues.

Some become Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four World-Protecting Kings; this is brought about by having previously heard of the merits of the Tathāgata-garbha. Their bodies are always peaceful and secure, free from illness and affliction; their lifespans are extended, and they are loved and respected by others. They fully hear the nectar-like Dharma of the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Great Parinirvāṇa, remaining firm, peaceful, and long-dwelling in the world, conforming to worldly ways while enjoying its company.

Knowing that all Tathāgatas do not arise from desire, they extensively reveal and expound this for the sake of the world; through the benefit of this wisdom and merit, wherever they are born, their descendants shall be numerous, their parents long-lived, and they shall constantly enjoy all the pleasures of humans and devas, possessing a preeminent and complete lineage—all this is due to hearing and knowing that all sentient beings possess the eternally abiding treasury of the Tathāgata.
In the future and the present, among gods and humans, they shall always be fully endowed with all forms of happiness because they have heard that the Tathāgata-garbha is eternally abiding.

Conversely, if those sentient beings—past, future, or present—within the five realms of existence are deficient in their limbs and members, and revolve through birth and death experiencing all manner of suffering, this is due to their disparaging and neglecting the Tathāgata-garbha.

If sentient beings have served various Buddhas through successive lifetimes, drawing near to them and making offerings, they will then be able to hear the Tathāgata-garbha; having faith and joyfully accepting it without giving rise to slander, if they can explain it with authentic consolation, you should know that such a person is indeed the Tathāgata.
If there are sentient beings who largely turn their backs on all Buddhas, they will give rise to slander upon hearing of the Tathāgatagarbha; those sentient beings burn their own seeds. Alas!
Alas! Alas! Those who lack faith are most pitiable throughout the three periods of time.
"All who preach the Dharma should speak in this manner, extolling the Tathāgata’s eternal and true reality.

If a preacher of the Dharma does not speak thus, they abandon the Tathāgatagarbha; such a person should not occupy the lion throne, just as a caṇḍāla should not don the robes or mount the elephant of a great king."

All Buddhas, through the utmost skillful means, seek the Tathāgatagarbha and find that it is not produced; this non-production is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs.

All Buddhas, through the most supreme skillful means, seek their own self-nature but find it unreal and unobtainable; this true nature is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs.

All Buddhas, through the utmost skillful means, seek a self-nature that is impermanent and find it unobtainable; the nature of permanence is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs.

All Buddhas, seeking through the most supreme skillful means, cannot find anything that is not eternal within the Tathāgatagarbha; this nature of eternity is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs of excellence.

All Buddhas, seeking through the most supreme skillful means, cannot find any changeability within the Tathāgatagarbha; this unchanging nature is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned with immeasurable marks and signs of purity.

All Buddhas, though seeking with the utmost skillful means, cannot find anything that is not quiescent within the Tathāgatagarbha; this very nature of quiescence is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned by the purity of immeasurable marks and signs.

All Buddhas, seeking through the most supreme skillful means, cannot find any destruction within the Tathāgatagarbha; this indestructible nature is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned with immeasurable marks and signs of purity.

All Buddhas, seeking through the most supreme skillful means, cannot find any destruction within the Tathāgatagarbha; its indestructible nature is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs.

All Buddhas, seeking through the most supreme skillful means, cannot find any illness within the Tathāgatagarbha; this nature of being without illness is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs.

All Buddhas, through their supreme skillful means, seek the Tathāgatagarbha and cannot find old age and death; the nature of being free from old age and death is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs. All Buddhas, through their supreme skillful means, seek the Tathāgatagarbha and cannot find defilement; the nature of being free from defilement is the Buddha-nature, which, within all sentient beings, is adorned with the purity of immeasurable marks and signs.

Just as oil mixed with water cannot be obtained [separately], so too the Tathāgata-nature is covered by immeasurable afflictions; it is impossible for the Buddha-nature to be mixed with afflictions, yet this Buddha-nature dwells within those afflictions.

It is like a lamp within a jar that becomes manifest when the jar is broken. Here, "jar" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), and "lamp" refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*. Regarding those who expound the *tathāgatagarbha*—whether they be Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, or Śrāvakas—the preachers may be either possessed of afflictions or free from afflictions, according to their respective capacities; this, Pūrṇa, you should know.

I say that such a person is one who has attained perfect awakening; they are able to shatter the jar of billions of afflictions of the recipient, and thereafter they are able to perceive their own nature as clearly as seeing an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand.
For example, when the sun and moon are shrouded by dense clouds, their radiance does not appear; yet once the cloud-obscuration is removed, their light shines forth clearly.

The Tathāgata-garbha is likewise: obscured by afflictions, its nature is not manifest; but upon emerging from afflictions, the great light shines everywhere, and the Buddha-nature is luminously pure, just like the sun and moon.
“Alas, Pūrṇa! You practice the conduct of a mosquito and do not know how to preach the Dharma; you should remain silent and depart quickly.

At that time, Sundarananda came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Seeing Aṅgulimāla, his heart felt sympathetic joy, and he praised him with a verse, saying:
“Excellent, Aṅgulimāla!”
"Having already cultivated sublime karma, you should now seek through skillful means the wondrous form-body of the Tathāgata.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla asked in verse:
"The World-Honored One has praised you, saying that your upright beauty is foremost."
What is it that makes one beautiful in this world, most exceptionally so?
By what cause does one attain such beauty?
Speak now to resolve our doubts.
At that time, Sundarananda replied in verse:
"Washing the hands and joining the ten fingers, Bowing one’s head to worship the Buddha’s relics,
Constantly making offerings to the sick— From these [practices], one attains physical comeliness."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke again in verse:
“The Buddha’s body has no sinews or bones; How could there be *śarīra* relics?
The Tathāgata is beyond relics; He is the supreme Dharma-body of skillful means.”
The Tathāgata is inconceivable; to cause those who have not yet believed to find faith and joy, he employs skillful means to manifest the existence of śarīra relics.
This skillful preservation of śarīra relics is the very nature of all Buddhas' Dharma.
Since time immemorial in this world, people have made offerings to Brahmā,
Maheśvara, devas, and devīs in various forms;
because these are not true refuges, they have erected śarīra-stūpas.
If there are sentient beings who understand these skillful means, they will,
by virtue of this wisdom of skillful means, attain a handsome and upright appearance.
It is not as you previously claimed— that the cause of such beauty lies in deluded conceptualization.
"Alas, Sundarī! You do not know the gateway to sublime beauty;
though you possess the form of a mere gnat, you are ignorant—silence would be fitting for you.

At that time, the Venerable Upāli approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Seeing Aṅgulimāla, his heart was filled with sympathetic joy, and he praised him in verse, saying:
"How marvelous, Aṅgulimāla!
You have already cultivated such extraordinary deeds; I now express my sympathetic joy. You should continue to cultivate the pure discipline.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla addressed him in verse, asking:
“The Tathāgata has praised you as the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.
How do you skillfully uphold the Vinaya?
Speak quickly to resolve our doubts.”
At that time, Upāli replied in verse:
"Do no evil whatsoever; Practice all virtues in their entirety;
Cultivate a pure mind through skillful means— This is how one properly upholds the Vinaya."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke again in verse:
“Those who destroy the Dharma and violate the precepts, These evil bhikṣus who do not follow the Vinaya—
One should confiscate their six requisites And all their means of livelihood.”

To inflict pressure, punishment, or expulsion, And to employ skillful means for the sake of subduing [the mind], These are the requisites for the holy life (brahmacarya); They are not things that violate the precepts.
Just as a great king Keeps a precious sword to protect his person,
If one is at a butcher’s shop, the Dharma dictates that one should take [the meat] by force;
for precious vessels belonging to a king should not fall into the hands of the wicked.
Such is the case for the requisites that a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārin) ought to accept and possess.
Not belonging to those who destroy the Dharma, he therefore gathers them back in;
this is called the foremost excellence in upholding the Vinaya in the world.
He does not commit a *duṣkṛta* offense, nor does he fail in proper decorum.
Thus is the upholder of the Vinaya, Fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s teaching.
The Tathāgata regards all beings Just as he does Rāhula;
Alas, Upāli! You have practiced the conduct of a mere gnat.
"One who does not understand how to properly uphold the Vinaya should remain silent out of ignorance.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Seeing Aṅgulimāla, his heart rejoiced, and he praised him in verse, saying:
"Excellent, Aṅgulimāla!"
"Having already cultivated sublime karma, you should now cultivate the Great Emptiness; all phenomena are non-existent.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla asked in verse:
"Mañjuśrī, Prince of the Dharma!
You see emptiness as foremost;
how do you regard the world? How do you well perceive the dharma of empty stillness?

That which is called the faculty of the eye is, in all Tathāgatas, eternal.
One clearly perceives with certainty, practicing fully without deficiency.
That which is called the faculty of the ear always hears with certainty and clarity from all Tathāgatas, practicing fully without deficiency.
That which is called the nose faculty, regarding all Tathāgatas, is always constant,
definitively clear smelling, and fully perfected without diminution.
That which is called the tongue faculty, regarding all Tathāgatas, is always constant...
With certainty and clarity he tastes, Fully perfected and without deficiency in his cultivation.
That which is called his body-faculty, Regarding all Tathāgatas,
always Touches with certainty and clarity, Fully perfected and without deficiency in its cultivation.
What are the six that are so named?
They are the six bases of sensory entry; these belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle and are not the Mahāyāna.
That which is called the eye-base is eternally present in all Tathāgatas.
Clearly seeing the gateway of the ear-faculty, one practices it fully and without deficiency.
Regarding the gateway of the ear-faculty, which is ever-present in all Tathāgatas,
one clearly hears its arrival and practices the gateway of the ear-faculty fully and without deficiency.
That which is called the sense-base of the nose is, for all Tathāgatas, eternal;
it is the gate of smelling that is clear and luminous, fully perfected and cultivated without diminution.
That which is called the sense-base of the tongue is, for all Tathāgatas, eternal.
The gate of clarity has entered; it is fully perfected and practiced without deficiency.
This is what is called the entrance of the body; it is ever-present in all Tathāgatas.
The gate of the contact of clarity has entered; it is fully perfected and practiced without deficiency.
What is called the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) is clearly taught as the Tathāgatagarbha;
without giving rise to a contrary mind, one enters the gate through pure faith.
What are the seven so named?
What are called the seven factors of enlightenment belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle; they are not the Mahāyāna.
The seven factors of enlightenment of the Mahāyāna are like the udumbara flower:
while the Tathāgata abides eternally, the wondrous flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment bloom.
What are the eight that are so named?
They are the Eightfold Noble Path; this belongs to the Śrāvaka vehicle and is not the Mahāyāna.
The Eightfold Noble Path of the Mahāyāna consists in hearing the teaching that the Tathāgata is eternal.
By the power of the causal condition of hearing this sutra, one will ultimately reach the city of Nirvana.
The Tathāgata is eternal and constant, supreme and unchanging;
he is pure, utterly tranquil, and the wondrous Dharma-body of Perfect Enlightenment.
The profound Tathāgatagarbha is ultimately free from aging and decay;
this is the Mahāyāna, which is fully endowed with the Eightfold Noble Path.
What are the nine?
What are called the ninefold scriptures constitute the Śrāvaka vehicle; these are not the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna is the One Vehicle, the unimpeded wisdom of the Tathāgata.
What are the ten? They are the so-called ten powers;
these belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle and are not the Mahāyāna.
Because the Mahāyāna possesses immeasurable powers, the Buddha is inconceivable.

Ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* worlds below here, there is a land named Constant Joyful King (*Nityapramuditārāja*). There, a Buddha named Severer of All Doubts (*Sarvasaṃśayacchedaka*) dwells and teaches. You should go there and ask that Buddha:
"Why does Śākyamuni Buddha dwell at the limit of the Adornment of Extensive Exposition, yet remains in the Sahā world without entering parinirvāṇa?"

"You, Aṅgulimāla, together with Mañjuśrī, should go to him and inquire about this matter. He will resolve all doubts for you; the Tathāgata shall speak for you, and because he is able to decisively sever all doubts, he is named the Buddha 'Severer of All Doubts' (Sarvasaṃśayacchedaka)."
At that time, Mañjuśrī and Aṅgulimāla together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent, excellent!”
“So be it; we shall receive your instruction.

Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he departed through the air like a king of geese and arrived at the realm of the Tathāgata King of Constant Joy. There he prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata Who Severs All Doubt, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed that Buddha, saying:

“We have come from the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha in the Sahā world, having traveled to the presence of the various Tathāgatas in ten worlds each throughout the ten directions, to inquire about this same meaning:”
"How is it that Śākyamuni Buddha dwells in the Sahā world without entering parinirvāṇa at the time of liberation?
All those Tathāgatas answered me, saying:
"Śākyamuni Buddha is our very selves; that Buddha himself shall resolve your doubts."
Śākyamuni Buddha has again sent me here to the presence of the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Tathāgata Who Severs All Doubts shall explain it for you.
For this reason, I now inquire regarding my doubts.
"How is it that Śākyamuni Buddha dwells in the Sahā world yet does not enter parinirvāṇa?
That Buddha replied, "Return; that Buddha himself shall resolve all your doubts."
"In this way, you are the emissary of the immeasurable Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
At that time, the two men both raised their voices and said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Very well, we shall receive your instruction.
Having paid homage at the feet of that Buddha and taken their leave, they returned to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha, prostrated themselves in worship, and spoke thus in praise:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni assumed immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodies and addressed me all at once, saying:
"Return, for the Buddha Śākyamuni shall resolve your doubts; that World-Honored One is none other than my own body."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī and the others, saying:
"Those Tathāgatas said to you:
'Am I indeed the body of those Tathāgatas?'"
Mañjuśrī and the others said: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"All Tathāgatas speak thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī and the others, saying:
"What are the worlds of those Tathāgatas like?"
Mañjuśrī and the others said: “In those worlds, there are no pebbles or gravel;

they are as level as clear water. Their touch is soft and pleasant like fine cotton wool. Like the Land of Peace and Bliss, they are free from the five turbidities, and there are no women, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas; there is only the One Vehicle, with no other vehicles.”
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the others, saying:

“If any son or daughter of good family should utter the names of all those Buddhas—whether reading them, writing them, hearing them, or even speaking of them in jest, whether to comply with others or to manifest their own excellence—then any terror or calamity that may arise shall be entirely extinguished. No devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, or the like, shall be able to disturb or harass them. Upon hearing [these names], they will be protected and the gates to the four miserable realms shall be closed. I say that even those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment thereby obtain the cause for bodhi; how much more so for those with pure hearts who read, recite, write, or hear them?”

Aṅgulimāla! The Tathāgata further possesses the power of extraordinary and great majesty, as taught in the Vaipulya-saṃgraha-mahādhāraṇī-sūtra: "The eighty billion Buddhas are all one Buddha, who is none other than my own body. Thus it is extensively taught. In this way, there are immeasurable Buddha-fields; in this way, there are immeasurable Tathāgatas; and in this way, the form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Tathāgata is infinite and boundless. Since the Tathāgata has accomplished such immeasurable merit, how could he be subject to impermanence or illness?
The Tathāgata abides eternally in a boundless body.

I shall now further explain in detail that there are fundamental bases, causes, and conditions: all Buddhas and all their causes do not delight in being born in this world, because these sentient beings are incurable.

For this reason, while I govern the sentient beings in this world who are difficult to cure, I repeatedly relinquish my physical body so as to give birth to a non-arising body, which subsequently corresponds to the body of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the unconditioned body (*anabhisaṃskāra-kāya*).

"Throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, I have sacrificed bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; because each of those bodies was wounded, beaten, or destroyed, I have now given birth to this indestructible, unconditioned body."

Throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and across numerous dwelling places, I have diligently sacrificed bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; because each body remained for immeasurable kalpas engaged in diligent ascetic practices, I have given birth to this body that does not age.

Throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have been born during eons of pestilence to act as an excellent medicine; because each of my successive bodies has persisted for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I am now born with a body free from disease.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have given rise to an immortal body in order to sever the disease of hunger for immeasurable sentient beings and to bestow upon them the flavor of the Mahāyāna.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have removed the defilements and impurities of immeasurable sentient beings; because I have manifested the Tathāgatagarbha for the sake of those who undergo difficult tasks, I have given birth to a body free from defilement.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have given rise to an outflow-free body (*anāsrava-kāya*) in order to eliminate the maladies of hunger and thirst of immeasurable hungry ghosts and to satisfy them with the flavor of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have maintained a mind of equal love and compassion toward all sentient beings—regarding them as my father, mother, son, elder brother, and younger brother—and for this reason, I have given birth to a body free from fault.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I established the truth of the Mahāyāna for immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans who spoke untruths, I have produced this body of eternal truth.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I have established immeasurable sentient beings, devas, humans, and those of non-Dharmic groups in the supramundane Dharma, this Dharmakāya has been produced.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, for the sake of establishing right view in immeasurable sentient beings—gods and humans—who followed false views, I have brought forth this foremost body of tranquility.

"Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I have established those immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans who were terrified in a state of fearlessness, I have produced a body of peace and security."

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I have established immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans who were filled with anxiety and distress in the Dharma free from anxiety and distress, I have produced this body that is without anxiety and detached from sorrow.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because I established all devas and humans who delighted in the lust of others in the great precepts and dignified conduct, I have produced this body that is stainless and free from dust.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, for the sake of gathering in and purifying immeasurable sentient beings of evil character and establishing them in the True Dharma, I have produced this dharma-body that is without weakness and free from frailty.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I bestowed the two treasuries of wealth and Dharma upon immeasurable sentient beings—gods, humans, and those who were impoverished—and established them in bodhi, I have given birth to a dharma-body free from calamity.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I have established immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans who follow desire and craving in the state of freedom from desire, I have produced this immeasurable body free from affliction.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have brushed away all the afflictions of immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans, just as one removes the venom of a snake; thus, I have given birth to this dharma-body, which is free from affliction and transcends suffering.
