Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have formed dharma-kinship with immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans; since no worldly intimacy surpasses that of dharma-kinship, I have given birth to this unconditioned, manifest, and wondrous body.

Throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, I have, for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans, expounded the Dharma of the pure Tathāgatagarbha in accordance with reality; therefore, I have produced this body of non-existence.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have established all devas and worldlings, causing them to abide in the rare and secret teachings of the Tathāgata; therefore, I have produced this rare body.

“Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because I have brought immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans to fulfillment through the Buddha’s power, I have produced immeasurable and boundless bodies of supreme excellence.”

Throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, I have manifested birth in various clans in every place in order to deliver immeasurable sentient beings; for this reason, I have produced this lofty body.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have caused immeasurable sentient beings to cross beyond all existence and establish them in bodhi; for this reason, I have attained the unsurpassed body.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have manifested with incomplete limbs and members in accordance with the world, in order to establish immeasurable sentient beings in Bodhi; thus, I have given birth to the unsurpassed Dharma-body.

Throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, across births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have never concealed the Tathāgata-garbha, which is my constant nature; for the sake of providing consolation and teaching to all sentient beings, I have taken birth in this body of constancy.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have maintained pure precepts; because I did not give rise to defiled thoughts upon seeing celestial maidens, demonesses, or women of the world, I have produced this body that is neither precarious nor fragile.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because I never gave rise to defiled thoughts toward women who were elders or superiors in any world, I have attained this body that does not collapse or decay.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, for the sake of removing the various ailments of immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans, I have brought forth this boundless and incomparable body.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I have established immeasurable sentient beings—even down to those in the animal realm—in the profound Dharma, I have produced this body of profound depth.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, for the sake of all devas and humans, I have taught that the Tathāgatagarbha is like the tracks of a bird in the sky, so as to cause the Buddha-nature to manifest; thus, I have taken birth in an invisible body.

“Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have turned away the views of self-clinging held by immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans, and have revealed the Tathāgatagarbha that is difficult to perceive; thus, I have manifested a body that is difficult for all sentient beings to see.”

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have produced subtle bodies for the sake of establishing all devas and humans in the True Dharma so that they do not harm sentient beings.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have brought all devas and humans the joy of the Dharma; therefore, I have attained a body of perfect fulfillment.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have universally revealed the Tathāgata-garbha to devas and humans, just as Mañjuśrī is seen now; therefore, I have attained a body that is not difficult to behold.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, for the sake of understanding the bonds of all sentient beings and establishing them in liberation, I have taken birth in bodies that are extremely difficult to behold.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas—whether among devas, humans, or the miserable realms, throughout all states of existence—I have dwelt universally therein, causing all beings to be established in true liberation; thus, I manifest the birth of non-dual bodies.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because I caused all devas and humans to purely uphold the five precepts, I was born with a body devoid of sinews and bones.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because I have skillfully made great vows to deliver all sentient beings, I have produced a body of liberation that appears in all places.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I have uprooted the arrows of all evil views from all sentient beings and established them in the true Dharma, I have produced this tranquil and immutable body.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have regarded all sentient beings equally as I do Rāhula; because I have also caused others to do so, I have produced this body of tranquil cessation.

“Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because I personally cultivated contentment and caused others to be content, I have given rise to a body of supreme tranquility (*upaśama*).

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because I preached to the śrāvakas on detachment from food and contentment, I have given rise to a body that has perfected the transcendence of severing all seeking.”

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have renounced all fish, meat, and delicacies, and because I have also taught sentient beings to renounce them, I have attained this exquisite body.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have caused immeasurable sentient beings—both devas and humans—to vomit up all afflictions; therefore, I have produced this body that is free from falsehood.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because I destroyed the dwellings of immeasurable sentient beings of evil character and drove them out from among the masses—just like fire or hail—I was born with a body like a ruined house.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I have caused immeasurable sentient beings who were deluded by the four inversions to drink the flavor of the Dharma, they have been born with bodies of Brahmā free from pride.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because the Tathāgatagarbha of immeasurable sentient beings is the quiescent, eternal Way, and because it utterly brings about the true and correct by departing from the faults of disorder, I have given rise to the body of quiescent relinquishment.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, for the sake of those immeasurable sentient beings who do not accept the Buddha’s teaching that there is no self, I established the existence of a self—like a finger pointing at the moon—and thus gave rise to the relinquishing of the body.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have entered parinirvāṇa after parinirvāṇa; yet, because I do not enter parinirvāṇa through parinirvāṇa, I give birth to the Dharma-body that accords with the Dharma.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, until the very limit of all sentient beings, I have sought the defilements of the Tathāgatagarbha with every possible skillful means; because they cannot be found, I have taken birth in this realm.
"All sentient beings possess this realm entirely.

Throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have manifested births to expound the Mahāyāna and the unimpeded wisdom of the true gateway of non-self and non-possessiveness; therefore, I have given birth to a body that has no place of entry."

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have brought immeasurable sentient beings to maturity so that they may fear their afflictions, thereby giving birth to the most excellent supramundane body.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have acted as a refuge for all sentient beings; because I have provided a reliance for those without reliance and kinship for those without kin, my birth has been like the myriad streams flowing toward the great ocean.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I have preached the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra with a fearless mind, I have given birth to a body that dwells in peace.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I have renounced supreme palaces, the sovereignty of a wheel-turning king, and immeasurable pleasures to enter the mountains and study the Way, I have given birth to a palace-body that is blissful and immovable.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have remained free from arrogance and laxity as if avoiding a *caṇḍāla*; because I did not even share a water vessel with those who maintain pure precepts, I have given rise to a body free from regret.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I lightened the heavy burden of afflictions of immeasurable sentient beings, I have produced a body of rest that is brilliantly radiant and clearly manifest.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, because I reviled the household life as being like dwelling in a prison, I have taken birth in the bodies sought by all sentient beings.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have caused immeasurable sentient beings to sever greed, anger, and ignorance; therefore, I have attained a body that is free from illness, free from fear, and free from the notion of "mine."

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have caused immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans to revile the afflictions of female dalliance as being like venomous snakes; for this reason, I have brought forth this body that undergoes extinction.

"Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, while practicing the bodhisattva path in the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpapradyota, I heard my own prediction of enlightenment. Because I have followed the Suchness and not slandered the sūtras, I have given birth to this house-like body."

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have heard that within the Tathāgatagarbha, all sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood upon severing all afflictions; because I believe in and rejoice in this, and because I protect sentient beings, I have given rise to the body of protection.

When I was a bodhisattva, throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, by practicing the patience of a rishi and cultivating the four immeasurables, I produced a body that serves as a refuge for all sentient beings.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have constantly expounded for immeasurable devas and worldlings the unobstructed wisdom of the Mahāyāna, the One Vehicle, and the Supreme Vehicle, providing the ultimate illumination for all sentient beings regarding the vehicle toward which they should proceed. Having heard these teachings, they generate the body of one who proceeds [toward liberation] by means of this Mahāyāna, because it destroys immeasurable evils.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have praised the Tathāgatagarbha—the realm of peace, the realm of all sentient beings, the foremost realm, and the stainless—as being without conjunction; therefore, I have produced a body that is without conjunction.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, for the sake of causing immeasurable sentient beings, devas, and humans to enter the celestial abode of the Pure White Liberation, I have produced this supreme body that is vast, boundless, and all-encompassing.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I have regarded immeasurable sentient beings—whether male or female—as my parents, brothers, and sisters, I have produced the body of the unsurpassed father in all places.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, because I gave food to others with countless bodies during eons of famine, I have been born in all places with a body free from the afflictions of hunger and thirst.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings, I have disparaged the evil of the icchantikas to instill in them a sense of dread; thus, I have brought forth this body that renounces all existence.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have manifested infinite bodies of skillful means, dharma-bodies, and supreme medicinal tree-bodies; because I do not increase unwholesome causes, I give rise to all bodies of non-action and tranquil cessation.

"Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have delivered immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to extinguish their afflictions and revealing their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as if looking at an *āmra* fruit held in the palm of one's hand; therefore, I have given rise to the body of the path of cessation."

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, for the sake of countless sentient beings, I have reviled all that exists as being like four venomous snakes or like an empty bottle; therefore, I have produced a body free from sinews, veins, and marrow.

Throughout births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings, I have extinguished all existence and immeasurable afflictions; because I have attained the nirvana of the extinction of desire, I have given birth to this body of immovable bliss that is nirvana itself.
Aṅgulimāla! For immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have dwelt in all boundless places and yet continue to dwell here. Aṅgulimāla!
Nirvāṇa is liberation, and liberation is the Tathāgata.
*Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, Scroll Three;
*Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One! How marvelous is the Tathāgata!
To have compassion for all sentient beings is the most difficult of deeds.”
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:
"It is not that performing this foremost difficult task is what makes the Tathāgata so extraordinary; there is yet another foremost difficult task.

To comfort and teach this Mahāyāna sūtra—the Tathāgatagarbha, which is eternal and unchanging—during the final eighty years when the True Dharma remains in the world, is what is truly most difficult."
If there are sentient beings who uphold [the teachings] of their own kind, this too is extremely difficult.

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the teaching that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging—the Tathāgatagarbha—accord with it according to reality, this too is extremely difficult.
Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is difficult?”
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:
"It is as if the great earth were bearing four heavy burdens.
What are these four?"
"First, great waters; second, great mountains; third, grasses and trees; fourth, sentient beings.
Thus, this great earth bears these four burdens.
Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One.
The Buddha addressed Aṅgulimāla:
"It is not this great earth that bears the fourfold burden. Why is this?
Because there is yet another who bears the heavy burden."
Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying: “Who is it,
World-Honored One?”
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:

"When eighty years remain before the True Dharma disappears from the world, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of all sentient beings, shall expound the Tathāgata-garbha—the Tathāgata who is eternal and unchanging—and they shall bear four burdens."
What are these four?

They are those of a fierce and malevolent nature who constantly seek to inflict harm, disregarding their own survival and casting aside their very lives and bodies, yet insistently proclaiming that the Tathāgata-garbha is eternal, constant, and unchanging. This is called the first burden, heavier than the accumulation of all the mountains.

If one encounters those who resemble fierce demons and are not upāsakas, and they revile him with the insults of an icchantika, yet he is able to endure all that he hears—this is the second burden, heavier than the accumulation of all the great waters.

To be unable to preach the Tathāgatagarbha to kings, ministers, powerful generals, and their retinues, but to preach it only to those who are lowly, deformed, poor, and mendicant—this is the third burden, heavier than the entire mass of all sentient beings.

To dwell in poverty at the frontiers in places of much affliction, where clothing, food, medicine, and all necessities are coarse and inferior; where every sensation is painful and nothing is pleasant; where men are entirely slanderous and women have little faith; and where one cannot reside in prosperous cities or villages—this is the fourth burden, heavier than a pile of all the grass and wood in the world.
If one can bear these four heavy burdens, such a person is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is able to bear the great burden.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, during the final eighty years when the True Dharma is about to perish, sacrifices body and life to expound the Tathāgata’s eternal, unchanging Tathāgatagarbha, this is extremely difficult;
if they are further able to sustain those sentient beings, this too is extremely difficult.
"It is also extremely difficult for those sentient beings to hear the teaching that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging—the Tathāgatagarbha—and yet to give rise to faith and joy.
Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla!"
It is not that this is the most difficult task for the Tathāgata; I shall now speak further of another even more difficult matter.

Suppose there were a man with an immeasurable lifespan who, after passing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of years, took a drop of water from the great ocean with the tip of a single hair. After passing through that same number of years again, he took another drop with a hair until the ocean was nearly exhausted, leaving only as much as a cow’s footprint. Would this not be extremely difficult?
Aṅgulimāla said: “It is extremely difficult, World-Honored One!
It is beyond description.”
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla, "This is not difficult;
there is something even more difficult.
Aṅgulimāla said:
"Who is it? World-Honored One!
The Buddha addressed Aṅgulimāla:

"When the True Dharma remains in the world for another eighty years, if there should be a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, renouncing body and life, expounds the Tathāgata-garbha as the eternal and unchanging Tathāgata, this is extremely difficult."
"Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla!
It is not that performing the foremost difficult task is what the Tathāgata considers difficult; there is an even more difficult task. Aṅgulimāla!"

“Suppose a man were to carry Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, along with the great earth and the vast oceans for ten billion years; would this not be considered the greatest strength and the most difficult feat?
Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying, “It is so.
Such is the realm of the Tathāgata; it is not something that can be attained by those śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla: "That is not of great power, nor is it particularly difficult. Suppose one were to take a single mote of dust from the great ocean and divide it into hundreds of thousands of billions of parts; then, for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, one were to carry away one such mote until the ocean was nearly exhausted, leaving only as much as a cow’s footprint.

Furthermore, suppose one could lift and carry the King of Mountains, Sumeru, along with the great earth, its rivers, and oceans for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas. Yet, compared to this, that person cannot be said to have achieved anything difficult if they are unable, during the remaining eighty years before the True Dharma vanishes from the world, to expound the Tathāgata’s eternal and unchanging Tathāgatagarbha. Only a Bodhisattva, a hero among men, can proclaim the Tathāgata’s eternal and unchanging Tathāgatagarbha and uphold the True Dharma; of such a person, I say that he has accomplished the foremost and most difficult task."
"Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla!
Suppose there were a man who could extinguish with water the blazing, raging fires of a trichiliocosm; would such a man not be most extraordinary?"
Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To extinguish the fires of even a single world-system is already extremely difficult, let alone those of a trichiliocosm.”
"This is indeed most difficult.
The Buddha said, "So it is."

Aṅgulimāla! In future ages, when those who uphold the precepts diminish and those who violate them increase, and when eighty years remain before the True Dharma disappears from the world, there will be Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who sacrifice their bodies, lives, slaves, cattle, sheep, and unrighteous wealth to proclaim the True Dharma with all kinds of purity, expounding the Tathāgata’s eternal, immutable Tathāgatagarbha. What kind of person is this?
Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Only the Buddha can know this; it is not within the scope of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, even to uphold the pure dharmas of the world is already difficult, let alone the supramundane, most excellent Tathāgatagarbha—the Tathāgata which is eternal, constant, and unchanging."
Just as it would be extremely difficult for a man to extinguish the blazing, intense fires of a trichiliocosm with water, so too,

if during the final eighty years when the True Dharma remains in the world, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should sacrifice his life and body to expound the Tathāgata-garbha— the eternal and unchanging nature of the Tathāgata— it should be known that such a person is himself the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to Aṅgulimāla:
“Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!”
I also speak thus: all Tathāgatas declare that the difficult deeds performed by that man have no limit.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Just as when the hundred rivers enter the great ocean, their individual currents no longer appear, so too, when all persons enter into the wisdom attained by such a man, they all cease to appear.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as the great ocean does not tolerate a corpse, so too this person—free from frivolous conduct, household attachment, domestic illness, and the confusion of unrighteousness—does not dwell together with those who slander the *tathāgatagarbha*. Such a person is exceedingly rare; likewise, it is also extremely difficult to sustain such a multitude and to serve as their listeners of the Dharma."
Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many marks must a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplish to be called one who is not a beginner?”
The Buddha addressed Aṅgulimāla, saying: "Good son,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes eight characteristics is not a beginner."
What are the eight? First, knowing the Dharma;

second, knowing how to contemplate and uphold it; third, making offerings to one's parents; fourth, recognizing the kindness of one's teachers; fifth, wearying of all evil views; sixth, distancing oneself from all forms of contemptuousness, lack of self-restraint, unwholesomeness, and impurity; seventh, not thinking of sensual desires, such that even in dreams no such thoughts arise; eighth, revering and honoring the precepts.
Thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes these eight characteristics is not a beginner.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes these eight characteristics is not a beginner.
What are the eight? First, preaching the Mahāyāna;

second, clearly expounding the Tathāgatagarbha without weariness or abandonment; third, not coveting wealth or material goods; fourth, practicing loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, and patience; fifth, regarding all sentient beings as if they were one's only child; sixth, associating with virtuous friends; seventh, distancing oneself from evil associates; eighth, being content with worldly gains.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these eight characteristics, they are not a beginner.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva accomplishes these eight characteristics, they are not a beginner.

What are the eight? First, comforting others with measured and beautiful speech; second, refraining from frivolous play; third, enduring afflictions with minimal defilement; fourth, enduring the hearing of all sūtras; fifth, subduing sleep; sixth, being free from indolence; seventh, exerting oneself with diligence and non-negligence; eighth, constantly delighting in seeking the precepts.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these eight characteristics, they are not a beginner.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva accomplishes these eight characteristics, they are not a beginner.

What are the eight? First, truthfulness; second, purity and delighting in the practice of pure deeds; third, radiance; fourth, physical comeliness; fifth, staying far away from women; sixth, staying far away from kinsmen; seventh, being terrified by hearing of evil and being so disturbed by various afflictions that one's body hair stands on end; eighth, compassion for sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these eight characteristics, they are not a beginner.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva accomplishes these eight characteristics, they are not a beginner.

What are these eight? First, skillfully knowing the distinction between what the Buddha has spoken and what Māra has spoken; second, reverently honoring those who know the sūtras; third, knowing the distinction between what is discipline and what is not discipline, as well as the two types of concealment; fourth, skillfully knowing the Tathāgata’s teachings of intentional concealment; fifth, knowing the Tathāgata’s secrets; sixth, skillfully knowing how to accord with worldly affairs; seventh, skillfully knowing that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging; eighth, skillfully knowing which matters regarding bodhisattvas are faults and which are not, and being naturally capable through knowledge of time and place.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these eight signs, they are not a beginner.
When they accomplish these forty signs regarding the mindfulness of the body and dharmas, this bodhisattva is not a beginner.

If they lack these forty merits, or even if they possess only half of them, you should know that such sons and daughters of good family do not abide in the Mahāyāna, nor do they enter the ranks of the bodhisattvas.
Therefore, the practice of a bodhisattva is exceedingly difficult.
What are those superior merits?
It is said that even in dreams they do not give rise to thoughts of desire; one should know that such a person possesses the supreme merit of all factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
At that time, Mañjuśrī said to Aṅgulimāla:
"What is the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*?

If all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*, then all sentient beings should become Buddhas; yet all sentient beings also commit unwholesome karmic traces such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking alcohol."
Why is this? Because all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and shall, at one and the same time, attain liberation.
If they possessed Buddha-nature, they would commit the five heinous crimes and become icchantikas.
If there were a self and a realm of self, one would have to cross over all existence.
Therefore, in this world, there is no self and no realm of self; that all dharmas are without self is the teaching of all Buddhas.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"All sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha, yet it is shrouded by immeasurable afflictions, like a lamp inside a jar."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! It is like this:
suppose there were a son of a disciplined family, for whom the Tathāgata Kāśyapa gave a prophecy, saying:
"Seven years from now, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja) who governs by the True Dharma; and I, too, seven days from now, shall enter Parinirvāṇa."
When the Son of the Tamer heard this prophecy, he was filled with joy and exultation, and thought to himself:
"The Omniscient One has prophesied that I shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; of this I have no doubt."
He then said to his mother, "Give me fish, meat, milk, curd, sesame, beans, and various kinds of fine food; then I shall have the strength.
Because he ate those mixed foods including meat, he was unable to sustain himself and died prematurely.
"What do you think, Mañjuśrī?
Is that Buddha a speaker of falsehood?
Or is he not omniscient?"
“Is it that those sentient beings truly lack the roots of goodness and the karmic fruit of a Wheel-Turning Sage King?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
"It was because of his original evil karma that he met this death.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "Do not speak thus;
he died at an untimely hour, but it was not due to the retribution of original evil karma."
Mañjuśrī! Did that Buddha bestow the prediction upon him without knowing of his past evil karma? He had no prior evil karma;
it was simply because he committed a transgression himself in the present that he met with the loss of his life.
In this way, Mañjuśrī!
If a man or a woman should think:
"Within my body there is the Tathāgatagarbha; I shall naturally attain liberation, so I may commit evil."
"If one who commits such evil deeds is able to attain liberation through the Buddha-nature,
or unable to attain it?
As stated above regarding that 'tamed son,' although he truly possessed the nature of a king, he was not able to attain liberation."
Why is this? It is because of their great heedlessness.
The Buddha-nature not delivering [sentient beings] is likewise so, because those sentient beings are greatly heedless.
Do all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature?
Or does it truly exist, like the retribution of a wheel-turning monarch?
Or is it that the Buddha has spoken falsely?

“Sentient beings engage in false speech and various forms of negligence; because they are negligent regarding the hearing of the Dharma and due to their own transgressions and evils, they cannot attain Buddhahood.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Do all sentient beings lack fundamental karma?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"They do possess fundamental karma; however, by hearing even a little of this sutra, immeasurable and incalculable transgressions are entirely eradicated."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, made this great vow:
"I shall cause all sentient beings who have not yet been delivered to be delivered; I shall cause all those who have not yet been liberated to be liberated."
"By the roots of goodness from this vow, and illuminated by the light of the Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sins shall all be completely extinguished.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!"

For example, when all clouds and mists have passed over and before the sun has risen, they completely obscure the entire world; yet once a small amount of sunlight emerges, all the darkness and obstructions of the world are entirely extinguished.
Thus, while this sūtra has not yet appeared, an accumulation of incalculable great sins causes all sentient beings to wander in the cycle of birth and death;

yet once this sūtra appears as the sun, even an accumulation of incalculable evil and great darkness is entirely extinguished in the mere blink of an eye. Within the Tathāgata-garbha—which is the Tathāgata’s eternal and unchanging nature—whether one speaks with playful jest or in conformity with others, or whether one commits the grave offenses of pārājika or the immediate retribution (ānantarya), these incalculable sins are all utterly destroyed in an instant. Furthermore, even those outside the Way [are likewise purified].
Why is this so? If one hears the name of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, although they have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment, they are already a bodhisattva. Why is this so?

Because the Tathāgata’s supreme vow holds that all worlds are his own, he shall cause those who have not yet been delivered to attain deliverance, and transform them through the True Dharma so that they may all achieve awakening.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī!
Those who hear the name of the Tathāgata are all bodhisattvas; not only can they swiftly eliminate their own afflictions, but they shall also attain the body that I have attained.
Mañjuśrī! As I have said in verse:
"I have already proclaimed the Path; The poisonous thorns of grief and sorrow have been extracted."
"You all should practice that which has been taught by the Tathāgata.
"When I speak of 'the path,' what path am I speaking of?
There are two kinds of paths: namely, the path of the śrāvaka and the path of the bodhisattva."
That which is the path of the śrāvaka refers to the Eightfold Noble Path;
that which is the path of the bodhisattva refers to the fact that all sentient beings possess the tathāgatagarbha.

By gradually severing all afflictions, I shall attain the Buddha-nature, which is immovable, blissful, and most worthy of being cherished; if one does not sever them, one will perpetually revolve in birth and death.

"I have already proclaimed the Way, and the poisonous thorn of sorrow and lamentation has been extracted. "Sorrow and lamentation" refers to the meaning of afflictions (*kleśa*); "extracting the thorn" refers to the Tathāgata.
I have severed immeasurable afflictions and am the Great King of Physicians; you should receive [the teaching] from me, for I shall show you the Tathāgatagarbha.
"‘You should act thus’ is a teaching spoken with intentional concealment.
‘That which was taught by the Tathāgata’—this is deceiving you, deceiving you."

The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as rare as the *udumbara* flower; gaining faith is like finding grains of gold in the sands of the Ganges, or like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log. Thus, encountering this *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—is not a deception regarding the fruits of one's life or lifespan within birth-and-death. It enables one to personally deliver oneself from all existence and the sickness of all afflictions; therefore, it is said to be "that which is spoken by the Tathāgata."
“Exert yourselves in all wholesome dharmas, Subdue all unwholesome states of mind;
Those who are slow in cultivating merit Will find their minds attached to evil.”
“This verse was spoken by me for the sake of the śrāvakas.

Furthermore, the Tathāgatagarbha is exceedingly difficult to encounter; there is nothing in the world so difficult to encounter as the analogy of the Tathāgata-garbha. You should quickly investigate it in this way: those whose minds are habituated to evil attachments, O bhikṣus, possess a naturally pure mind that is surrounded from before and after by numerous afflictions, with the five defilements at their head, due to the fault of associating with evil spiritual friends.”
What are the five defilements that serve as the root, surrounded by all afflictions?
They are namely: greed, anger, sloth, restlessness, and doubt.

These five defilements corrupt the mind. Those who wish to purify the root of these five defilements and all afflictions should diligently apply skillful means through the power of the intrinsically pure mind; they should diligently apply skillful means while the Sūtras have not yet been slandered and before becoming an icchantika; they should diligently apply skillful means to practice for their own liberation.
For this reason, it is said that the mind is afflicted by immeasurable adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*), and one should swiftly and urgently uproot their very foundation:
"Mind precedes all phenomena; mind is supreme, mind is born [from them]; if one has pure faith in the mind, phenomena follow accordingly."
"Whether one speaks or acts, happiness follows of its own accord, like a shadow follows the form.
This verse was spoken by me for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle;
its intended meaning refers to the Tathāgatagarbha.
If the naturally pure mind is the Tathāgatagarbha, it is superior to all phenomena, for all phenomena are produced by the Tathāgatagarbha;
and because the dharma of the mind of pure faith cuts off all afflictions and perceives the realm of the self.

If one possesses pure faith that the *tathāgatagarbha* exists within oneself, then whatever one speaks or does will lead to the attainment of Buddhahood; and when one has become a Buddha, whatever one speaks or does will deliver all the world, just as a person sees their own reflection. Seeing the *tathāgatagarbha* is likewise so; therefore, it is said that it follows the form like a shadow.
“Mind precedes all phenomena; mind is supreme, mind-born.
If one speaks or acts with an evil mind, suffering follows, as surely as the wheel follows the hoofprint of the ox.”
"This refers to a single-pole, two-wheeled cart drawn by two oxen, such that the wheels follow the tracks.
This verse explains the meaning of afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for 'the mind and mental factors being evil,' it means that because they are shrouded by immeasurable afflictions and thereby produce various evils, they are called 'evil.'"

Not knowing that the self-nature of the mind is the *tathāgatagarbha*, one enters into the realm of immeasurable afflictions; because such agitation and turbidity do not cease, whether speaking or acting, all manner of suffering constantly follows without end.

As for "the wheel following the tracks": the accumulation of all evils and the cycle of birth and death turn all sentient beings within the three evil realms, like a wheel following its tracks. Therefore it is said that those whose merit is slow are inclined in their hearts toward unwholesome dharmas.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Just as one knows that there is ghee in milk, so one employs skillful means to churn and seek it, yet does not churn water because there is no ghee in it."
In this way, Mañjuśrī,
because sentient beings know that the Tathāgatagarbha exists, they apply themselves with diligence to maintaining the precepts and purely cultivating the holy life.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Just as one knows there is gold in a mountain and thus digs into the mountain to seek the gold, rather than digging into a tree because it contains no gold; so it is, Mañjuśrī!
Because sentient beings know that the Tathāgatagarbha exists, they diligently uphold the precepts and purely cultivate the Brahma-faring, saying:
"I shall certainly attain the path of Buddhahood. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
"If there were no Tathāgatagarbha, one would practice the pure life (brahmacarya) in vain; it would be like drilling water for an entire kalpa and never obtaining ghee.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of the holy life (brahmacarya)?
For what reason does the Tathāgata renounce the pleasures of the five desires?
Aṅgulimāla said to Mañjuśrī:
"Immeasurable devas and humans always know that they are subject to the law of falling [into lower realms], and therefore they remain free from all thoughts of desire.
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:
"Do not speak such words."
"All sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha; all men are brothers, and all women are sisters.
Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"How is it that King Śuddhodana and Queen Māyā, who were brother and sister, became father and mother?
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:
"This was a skillful manifestation to deliver sentient beings; had it not been so, they could not have been delivered."

It is like a great king who has two thousand strongmen; these two men employ skillful means to manifest a display of subduing one another, thereby pleasing the king’s heart and entertaining the multitude, yet they alone know this while no others can perceive it.

The Buddha is likewise: he manifests through his parents to appear as a human being, and only thereafter does he deliver immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to emerge from the boundless great ocean of birth and death, yet those sentient beings are unable to know this.
For example, just as an actor among a great assembly manifests various transformations to delight the minds of the multitude,
so too do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifest various transformations to deliver sentient beings, yet those sentient beings are unable to know them.
For example, it is like a magician who, in the midst of a great assembly, severs his own limbs to delight the people, yet in reality his body suffers no injury or loss.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are also like this; they manifest various transformations, just like that magician, in order to deliver sentient beings.

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, with his omniscience, knows all things; he observes that among all sentient beings in the world, there has been none who has not been one's father, mother, brother, or sister since beginningless time. Their births and deaths are impermanent as they alternate between high and low status and the roles of superior and inferior, just like a performer who repeatedly changes costumes. For this reason, the Tathāgata purely cultivates the brahma-faring.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
These and those [beings] take pleasure together within their own realms; how do they experience such joy?
Why is it that the remaining parts of the body are not obtained, and why do they not constitute the retribution of the realm?"
You should know that this pleasure is a great mass of suffering; women possess the Buddha-treasure, and men are likewise so.
Why do you, being of one nature, become defiled by attachment?
Because of this single nature, the Tathāgata has purely cultivated the Brahma-faring, abiding in his own ground and the ground of non-retrogression, thereby attaining the ground of the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the Tathāgata not establish upāsakas and upāsikās by means of all the pure practices (brahmacarya)?”
For what reason, World-Honored One,
do you say that bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās are the causes of the True Dharma, like the four pillars of a hall?
"Now, why is it that upāsakas and upāsikās who currently manifest great evil are established within the True Law and Discipline?

The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "This 'differentiated thought' is called a worldly thought. The Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as Rāhula; he constantly desires to establish them so they may abide in the stage of Buddhahood without such gradual progression. The Buddha-thought differs from this worldly thought; to differ from this is what is called a non-questionable discourse."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
because the realm of all sentient beings is a single realm, do the Buddhas refrain from taking life?”
The Buddha said:
"It is so. Killing in the world is like a person killing themselves, for one kills that which belongs to one's own realm."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
for what reason do you regard all sentient beings as Rāhula, yet further instruct people to subdue, kill, or punish those of various evil types within their own realms?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Good son, do not speak in this way.”
The Tathāgata regards all sentient beings in this way, just as he regards Rāhula.

For example, suppose a man who normally eats twice a day, out of a love for the Dharma, were to eat only once a day; he would thereby kill eighty thousand families of worms. In such a case, it should be called "killing," yet it is not the impurity of killing.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! Boundless sensual desires are that which the noble ones renounce.

If one were to say that noble persons harm themselves for the sake of destroying desire, then noble persons would incur the fault of self-harm; that is, when the mind of craving is intense, they go to others and say:
"I have given rise to a lustful mind; I pray you instruct me so that shame and remorse may arise. Whether I live or die is of no consequence, for I shall then use skillful means to take my own life."
“Is one who acts in this way harming their own realm?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
He shall, by means of these merits, increase his accumulation.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"So it is, Mañjuśrī! For what reason do the noble ones take their own lives?"
Since this is the case even for one's own poisonous snake of afflictions, how much more so for the bodies of others?

Regarding the teachings spoken by the Buddha, when those of evil character who destroy the True Dharma are full of their own afflictions, to instruct and admonish them and create various difficulties for them is to make an offering to one’s own realm. Just as one seeks ultimate happiness for oneself by renouncing the pleasures of desire, food, clothing, and life, and just as one subdues others by harming one’s own body, this is called "skillfully knowing the Tathāgata-garbha."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is it because of the Tathāgatagarbha that the Buddhas do not eat meat?”
The Buddha said: "It is so.

Throughout the beginningless cycle of birth and death, there is not one among all sentient beings who has not been their father, mother, brother, or sister. Just as an actor changes roles, things are impermanent; one's own flesh and the flesh of another are but the same flesh. For this reason, all Buddhas do not eat meat."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
The realm of all sentient beings and my own realm are one and the same realm; the flesh in which they dwell is one and the same flesh. For this reason, all Buddhas do not eat meat.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are conch shells, cowries, beeswax, honey, leather, and silk not the flesh of their own realms?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Do not speak such words.
The Tathāgata is far removed from all worldly things; the Tathāgata does not eat. It is impossible that he would associate with worldly objects."

If it is something acquired through habitual association, that is a method of acquisition; if an object comes to one through successive transfer, it may be accepted. However, if an object comes from its place of origin, it may not be accepted; yet if it has come through successive transfer and is removed from the hand of the killer, it may be accepted.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In this city there is a cobbler who can make leather sandals. If someone were to buy them and offer them as a gift, which have come down through successive hands, would the Buddha accept them?"
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Suppose there is a cow that has died of itself, and the owner takes its hide from a caṇḍāla and gives it to a leather-worker to have made into sandals, which he then offers to a person who upholds the precepts. Is it appropriate to associate with such a thing as it comes through this succession?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“If a cow dies naturally and its owner takes the hide to make leather sandals, which he then gives as a gift to one who upholds the precepts, should that person accept them?”
"If not receiving [the gift] is the dharma of a bhikṣu, then to receive it would not be compassion; yet, it does not constitute a violation of the precepts.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Furthermore, one must not cook food with impure water, nor should a bhikṣu accept it; if one acts in such a manner, this is what is manifested.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“This is called a worldly notion.”
If there were upāsakas, one could not use water purified by them for food;
if there were no upāsakas, what would become of the Buddhas?

If land-dwelling creatures, water-dwelling creatures, and even those in the void are likewise [sentient beings], then this would be detrimental to the Pure Land school; how, then, could one cultivate the Pure Land school in the world?
This is called a "fallacious argument" (*avijñāta-vyākaraṇa*).
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For a long time, the world has also established for itself the practice of not eating meat.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
“If there are those in the world who accord with the Buddha’s words, you should know that they are all the Buddha’s words.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The world also speaks of liberation, yet that liberation is not true liberation; only the Buddha-dharma is liberation.
There is also that which is called ‘leaving home,’ yet it is not true leaving home; only the Buddha-dharma is true leaving home.”
"World-Honored One!

In the world it is also said that 'I do not eat meat,' yet for them there is neither a self nor a non-eating of meat; only within the Dharma of the World-Honored One is there a self who resolutely does not eat meat."
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“Do you wish to hear about the causes for the establishment of non-Buddhist paths in the world?
I shall explain them for you.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
We joyfully desire to hear [it].”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Kuṇḍanābhadra who appeared in the world in this very city."

At that time, that world will be free of grit and pebbles; the name "non-Buddhist" (tīrthika) will not exist, and there will be only the Single Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), while all those sentient beings will experience constant happiness.

At that time, the Tathāgata will remain in the world for a long duration before entering parinirvāṇa. After his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma (saddharma) will remain for a long time, but when the Dharma is about to perish, those who uphold the precepts will diminish and those who act contrary to the Dharma will increase.
There was an araṇya bhikṣu named Buddhajñāna; a virtuous person offered him a priceless robe, and out of compassion for that person, the bhikṣu accepted it.

Having received it, the bhikṣu showed it to the hunters. When the group of hunters saw this fine garment, they conceived the intent to rob him; that very night, they took the bhikṣu into the deep mountains, mangled his body, stripped him naked, and hung him from a tree by his hands.

At that time, during the night, there was a flower-gathering brahmin who went to the aranya and saw a tiger; terrified, he fled toward the mountains. There he saw that bhikṣu with his body mangled, naked, and with his arms outstretched tied to a tree.
Having seen this, he cried out in astonishment: "Alas, O śramaṇa!"
"Previously he wore the *kāṣāya*, but now he is naked; he must have realized that the *kāṣāya* is not the cause of liberation, and that self-inflicted asceticism is the true way to study the Path.

That person would surely abandon the wholesome Dharma, thinking clearly that this is the cause of the path to liberation; because he destroys the True Dharma, he discards his robes and plucks out his hair to become a naked ascetic (*nagna-śramaṇa*), and from this, the tradition of the naked ascetics arose.

At that time, having himself attained liberation from bondage, the bhikṣu took tree bark and dyed it with red ochre to clothe himself, and tied grass together to make a whisk for brushing away mosquitoes and insects.
Furthermore, a flower-gathering Brahmin, having seen this, thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu has discarded his former fine robes and wears such garments and holds such a whisk."
"How could that person possibly abandon the wholesome dharmas? One should know for certain that this is the path to liberation.
He then studied that dharma, and from this point on, the renunciant Brahmins arose.
At that time, the bhikṣu entered the water at dusk to bathe; while washing his head wound, he took some water-weeds to cover the wound and gathered discarded rags left by cowherds to clothe his body.
At that time, a woodcutter saw this and thought to himself:

"This bhikṣu previously wore the kāṣāya, but now he has discarded it entirely; he must know that the kāṣāya is not the cause of liberation, which is why he wears his hair loose, dresses in rags, and practices asceticism by bathing three times every day and night."
"How could that person ever abandon the wholesome dharmas? One should know clearly that this is the path to liberation.
He then studied those teachings, and from this arose the ascetic Brahmins.

After the bhikṣus had bathed, their bodies were covered with many sores that flies and bees swarmed and fed upon. They immediately smeared white ash over the sores in various places and covered their bodies with wet rags.
Those who saw them at that time said, "This is the Way."
He immediately studied that dharma; thus arose the practice of the ash-smearing Brahmins.
At that time, the bhikṣu kindled a fire to cauterize his ulcer, but the pain of the ulcer became so unbearable that he threw himself from a cliff to take his own life.
At that time, those who saw this thought to themselves:
"This bhikṣu previously wore fine robes, yet now he is like this.
Could it be that he has abandoned the wholesome Dharma? One should know that throwing oneself from a cliff is the path to liberation."
"From this point on, the practices of throwing oneself from cliffs and worshipping fire arose.
Thus, among these ninety-six types [of sects], all arose because of this bhikṣu’s various forms and appearances, giving rise to manifold delusions and each producing their own views."

It is like a country where people look at one another and give rise to coarse thoughts; once these coarse thoughts have arisen, they kill one another. It is likewise with the ninety-six kinds of paths, each of which gives rise to different conceptions.
It is just as a thirsty deer, perceiving a mirage as water, pursues it until it dies of exhaustion;
when the True Dharma is extinguished, it is likewise for those bhikṣus who perceive what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma.
Thus it is, Mañjuśrī!

Among all that is done in the world, including the various practices of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and decorum, all are entirely manifestations of the Tathāgata. When the Dharma is about to perish, such things arise; if this is so, then the True Dharma is extinguished.
In this way, Mañjuśrī!

Regarding the true self in the world, such is the case; likewise, those various false views and deluded imaginings that claim liberation is thus, or that the self is thus transcendent from the world, do not understand the Tathāgata’s teaching of intentional concealment (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*). They claim that "non-self" is what the Buddha taught, yet they engage in conceptualization according to those words just as non-Buddhists do based on their causal theories.
Those in the various worlds follow along with ignorance, and even those who have transcended the world likewise lose their way, concealing and obscuring the teaching of wisdom.

For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of the Middle Way of the One Vehicle, which is free from the two extremes: "I am real; the Buddha is real; the Dharma is real; the Saṅgha is real. Therefore, he calls this Middle Way the Mahāyāna.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Sentient beings do not know the Middle Way; they falsely conceptualize and speak of other 'middle ways'."
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:
"Few sentient beings will hear this sutra and believe it; many future sentient beings will slander it.
Aṅgulimāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain: in which directions and how many sentient beings slander this sutra?
How many icchantikas are there? And in which directions are there those capable of extensively providing consolation and preaching it for the sake of sentient beings?”
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on us and explain this for us.
The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:
"In a future age, in the Middle Kingdom, there shall be nine hundred and eighty billion sentient beings who slander and destroy this sutra; seven billion sentient beings shall become icchantikas."
In the east, ninety-eight thousand koṭis of sentient beings slandered and rejected this sutra; sixty koṭis of sentient beings became icchantikas.
In the west, ninety-eight hundred koṭis of sentient beings slandered and rejected this sutra; fifty koṭis of sentient beings became icchantikas.
In the south, ninety-eight koṭis of sentient beings slandered and rejected this sutra; forty koṭis of sentient beings became icchantikas.
In the land of Kaśmīra, my remaining Dharma exists; in the land of Vāhīka, it is known by another name as "the Imperishable"; and it is likewise in the land of Vinataka.
In Kaśmīra, half of the bhikṣus practice the Mahāyāna, while the other half delight in the Mahāyāna and expound the Mahāyāna.

In the south, there shall be those who practice the path of firm resolve and the conduct of the Tathāgata; free from the eight great matters, they shall proclaim the Tathāgata-garbha as the eternal and unchanging nature of the Tathāgata. Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās shall practice this path of firm resolve and shoulder my Dharma.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How marvelous is the Buddha-dharma; it shall abide in the southern region.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “It is so, it is so.
My Dharma shall remain in the south for a short time.

Because you bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice asceticism do not begrudge your own bodies or lives and comfort all sentient beings, you preach the Tathāgata-garbha—the Tathāgata as eternal, constant, and unchanging—just as all Buddhas do. While none of the other Buddhas take pleasure in coming to this world to bear the burden of the immeasurable sentient beings of the trichiliocosm, I alone am able to deliver them here.”
When eighty years remain before the extinction of the True Dharma, I, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, likewise do not delight in upholding the True Dharma at that time.
"Mañjuśrī, it shall be as you have said!

When the True Dharma is about to perish, with eighty years remaining, at that time you shall take up the burden of the True Dharma throughout Jambudvīpa and all the other continents, expounding the Tathāgata’s eternal and unchanging Tathāgatagarbha without sparing your own body or life; at that time, sentient beings will either believe or disbelieve."
Those bodhisattvas form this thought:
"Even if my body were cut into various pieces, I shall thereby attain the eternally abiding body.

Like you, Mañjuśrī, and the other immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, who take up the burden of the True Dharma in that southern region—a task that is foremost and most difficult—I constantly praise the south as the place where the final teaching of the Dharma is proclaimed.

By the power of that bodhisattva’s majestic virtue, all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa and the intervals between the continents hear his name and dedicate themselves toward him, whether out of a sense of shame or out of fear.

It is like a king who, having heard the laws of other kings, governs his own kingdom; so too is it with the preaching of the Mahāyāna secret treasury out of a sense of shame and fear regarding the kingdom of Kaśmīra and the city of Kāruka-cakra—yet, they do not speak of the Tathāgata-garbha as the eternal and unchanging nature of the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī! It is like setting fire to a field of grass: it burns only the center and does not burn the periphery.

When my original place of birth was established, the path of cessation was firm; other dharmas remained at the southern periphery. That the various bodhisattvas there shoulder and uphold the True Dharma is likewise so; you should know that within that [periphery] there is a Tathāgata.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, together with his retinue of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, having made great offerings, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"We shall together protect and uphold this sutra; we pray that you will entrust it to us. We only wish that, out of compassion for all sentient beings, you would speak the name of this sutra.
The Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "Kauśika!..."
This sutra is named "Aṅgulimāla"; it should be upheld in this way.
Kausika! This sutra is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower.
At that time, the eldest son of Śakra, named Abhimanyu, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When my father, the King, was engaged in battle with the asuras, he said to his charioteer:”
"You must prepare the chariot for subduing the asuras.
The charioteer replied to the king,
"Please do not worry."

"I shall die first so that you may follow the King; now I must bring my life to an end with firm resolve for this decisive battle, and the others as well shall cast away their bodies and exhaust all their strength.
Thus it was, World-Honored One!

In a future age, during the eighty years when the True Dharma is about to perish, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas shall proclaim that the Tathāgata is eternal, constant, and unchanging, and that he is the Tathāgatagarbha.
Again, he thinks:
"When I preach the Dharma, there will be many sentient beings who cannot endure it; I shall not speak.

At that time, lest those sons of good family hear those difficulties and give rise to a mind of regression, one should know that they skillfully harness and adorn the vehicle of the Dharma, which is like the *tathāgatagarbha*. The Tathāgata is eternal, constant, quiescent, and unchanging, widely proclaiming this throughout the world; those sons of good family thus proclaim the *tathāgatagarbha* of the Tathāgata as eternal, constant, and unchanging.
"At that time, I shall become a bhikṣu and protect [the Dharma], even at the cost of my life.
Then, many sons of Śakra—whether male or female—as well as other devas, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and made this vow:
"We shall become bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, and protect [the Dharma], even at the cost of our lives."
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"

All of you are seekers of the True Dharma, and I too shall provide protection for all who delight in the Dharma. I shall always walk before you like a skilled charioteer; you, in turn, must always remain firm in your gratitude and extensively proclaim the Tathāgatagarbha—the abode of the Tathāgata, the eternal abode, the quiescent abode, the unchanging abode.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having arrayed his fourfold army, addressed his ministers, saying:

"There is now a man who resembles a rākṣasa, who has killed many people—one short of a thousand—making a garland of their fingers and smearing his body with their blood. Valiant, fierce, and swift, he has unleashed his violence within this realm. He is currently less than forty *go-vyūha* (cow-bellowings) from this city; he may yet harm me and my ministers and subjects to complete his tally. We must now go together to exterminate this murderous demon."
Now, within this city, all men and women who wish to seek anything do not dare to go out; even all the birds and beasts, upon hearing his evil name, do not venture there.
"You all must now issue a proclamation to both the inner and outer courts:

'King Prasenajit has now mobilized his fourfold army to punish that rākṣasa Aṅgulimāla. All of you must come bearing weapons. If you can fight against him with all your might, whether you are wounded or not, rewards shall be granted according to your merit—elephants, horses, precious jewels, cities, and lands; whatever you desire shall be given to you.'"
Hearing that evil reputation, there was none who did not tremble with fear; yet, when thus proclaimed, not a single person responded to the call.
Only those in the King’s retinue were unable to maintain their independence; constrained by his majestic countenance, they bowed and submitted in obedience.
At that time, the consorts and queens wept and remonstrated with him, saying:
"We would rather lose our royal positions than wish for you to lead an expedition yourself.
He immediately summoned the Grand Diviner to inquire about its auspiciousness or ill omen.
"Will you now be able to subdue Aṅgulimāla?
The diviners all replied,
"He shall be destroyed this very day."

Although he heard these words, the king still did not believe them; leading his fourfold army, he went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side with an expression of fear and perspiration flowing from his forehead.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the All-Knowing One who knows all things, knowing [the reason] yet asked intentionally:
"Great King,
for what reason are you sweating today?"

The king addressed the Buddha, saying: "There is currently a rākṣasa named Aṅgulimāla who has killed nine hundred and ninety-nine people. He wears fingers as a garland and smears his body with blood. Fearing that he will not cease his depredations and will come to wage war against me, all the people of the kingdom are terrified; they shut their doors and do not go out, and their livelihoods have been abandoned. Not a single bird or beast dares to approach him. I have prepared these fourfold armies and intend to go and punish him."
The Buddha said to the king,
"Does Your Majesty now wish to punish him?
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now, with a single mind, take refuge in the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"If Aṅgulimāla were to come here, what would you do?"
At that time, the fourfold army was all struck with great terror, yet the king alone felt no fear, for he relied upon the majestic power of the Buddha.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If those who come were as numerous as this, [it would still be but one."}
At that time, the World-Honored One pointed to him and said to the king, "This is Aṅgulimāla, the Ever-Victorious.

When the king beheld Aṅgulimāla staring fixedly without blinking, observing his appearance—his bloodshot eyes and heroic bearing—he was struck with such terror that his hair stood on end as if possessed by a non-human spirit. His fierce resolve subsided and his sword fell away of its own accord. He gradually approached the Tathāgata’s lion throne, and with single-minded sincerity, he took refuge in the Tathāgata, saying, "Please regard us as you do Rāhula."
At that time, the fourfold army became twice as terrified; bewildered and overwhelmed, they fled in all directions.
Then, the World-Honored One emitted the light of fearlessness that comforts sentient beings, illuminating those beings and causing their bodies to be at peace and happy.
At that time, King Prasenajit, his inner and outer retinues, and the people of the city all thought to themselves:
"Now Aṅgulimāla has been subdued by the World-Honored One."
King Prasenajit uttered these words of praise:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!

You are truly the foremost yoke of those who tame; you are truly the unsurpassed teacher of gods and humans. That one such as this, who committed such violent and great evil deeds, could be skillfully established in the True Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses in praise:
"One who was formerly heedless, but later ceases and does not transgress, illuminates the world like the moon when the clouds have vanished."

"If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva first manifests negligence and subsequently manifests merit, he illuminates the world like the moon when the clouds have vanished, delivering immeasurable sentient beings and manifesting the merits of a Tathāgata."
"Great King!
You should know that he is not an evil person; rather, this is simply the skillful means of a bodhisattva.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason do you say he is not an evil person?
Previously, he insulted his teacher's wife and practiced the wicked conduct of a *piśāca* under that evil teacher.
The Buddha told the Great King:

"He did not defile his teacher's wife, nor was he her teacher; yet, by manifesting the forms of that teacher and his wife, he transformed her mind. He practiced the teacher’s methods, claiming they were always pure."
"Great King, you should know!
This is most extraordinary and marvelous; it is like the collision of a dragon-elephant and a bull-elephant, which a donkey cannot endure.
Thus it is, Great King!"

The Tathāgata, the Great Elephant-King among men, has concealed his teachings and spoken them in secret; this is beyond the capacity of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and can only be borne by Buddha after Buddha.
"Great King!

To the south, passing from here through lands as numerous as the sands of sixty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Sarvaratnavyūha. There dwells a Buddha named Sarvalokapriyadarśana-mahāparākrama Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who remains in the world teaching and transforming beings. In that realm, there are no vehicles of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; it is purely the One Great Vehicle, with no other vehicle names remaining."

Those sentient beings therein are free from old age, illness, and any unpleasant suffering; they experience nothing but pure happiness. Their lifespans are immeasurable, their radiance is immeasurable, and their complexions are purely exquisite, such that there is nothing in all the worlds to serve as a simile. Therefore, the land is named "Adorned with All Jewels," and the Buddha is named "Supreme Great Diligence Delightful for All Worlds to Behold."
The King should rejoice, join his palms, and pay respectful homage. Could that Tathāgata be anyone else?
Aṅgulimāla is himself that Buddha; the realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable.
At that time, King Prasenajit said to the diviners:
"All of you have spoken falsehoods; depart quickly and do not speak such lies again."

At that time, the devas, humans, and nāgas, as well as the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, King Prasenajit, and all the people from the cities, towns, and villages, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, all assembled together. They prostrated themselves at the feet of Aṅgulimāla and, with one mind and in unison, spoke these verses of praise:
“Homage to the Tathāgata of Boundless Body! Homage to the skillful Aṅgulimāla!
I now prostrate at the base of your holy feet; I repent before the soft feet of the World-Honored One.”
I now repent before the Honored Tathāgata, Aṅgulimāla, who possesses a body of two births;
for our sake he has come here, manifesting the form and appearance of a Buddha with supreme radiant flames, illuminating all sentient beings and capable of preaching.
I repeatedly offer my prostrations and repentance to this immeasurable body.
The Perfectly Awakened One provides refuge to those without refuge; to those without kin, he acts as a kinsman.
How marvelous that two Buddhas have appeared in the world!
Such an unprecedented phenomenon has occurred in the world, like a lotus blooming within fire—rare indeed is the sight of two Buddhas in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit, saying:

"To the north, passing from here through lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Constant Joy. There dwells a Buddha named Joy-Treasury Maṇi-Ratna-Accumulation Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who remains in the world teaching and transforming."

In that land there are no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; it is purely and solely the Mahāyāna, with no names for other vehicles. Furthermore, there are no names for the various sufferings of old age and illness; it is purely and solely bliss. Their lifespans are immeasurable and their radiance is immeasurable, beyond all comparison; therefore, the country is named Constant Joy (Nityapramudita).
The Buddha is named Ratinidhānagarbha-maṇirāśi Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; Your Majesty should rejoice with palms joined in reverence.
Could that Tathāgata be anyone else? It is none other than me.
Mañjuśrī is that very Buddha.

If there are sentient beings who pay reverent homage to Aṅgulimāla and Mañjuśrī, or even those who merely hear the names of these two, they will see the Land of Joy as if seeing their own home. Because they have heard those names, the four evil realms are forever closed to them. Whether it be out of playful jest, compliance with others, or for the sake of fame and profit—whether they be followers of this path or external paths, or even those who have committed grave prohibitions or the five sins of immediate retribution—the four evil realms shall likewise remain closed to them.

If good sons or good daughters are protected by these two names, then in the present and in future lives, they shall receive protection in all wildernesses, treacherous places, and locations of terror; in all such places, their fears shall be entirely extinguished, and neither devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, nor piśācas shall be able to cause them harm.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit:

"What the Tathāgata has spoken possesses such great majestic power; the conduct of Bodhisattvas possesses such great majestic power; and Mañjuśrī as well as Aṅgulimāla possess such great majestic power. By giving rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward these two nāgas, one can initiate the immeasurable practices of a Bodhisattva."
"Great King!
You should provide for and support Aṅgulimāla’s mother; do not forget her.
This mother of Aṅgulimāla is protected by my skillful means."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla’s mother rose into the air to a height of seven tala trees and spoke these verses:
“What the Tathāgata has manifested, all sentient beings do not know;
the illusion created by the Tathāgata is the king among all illusions.”
“The body of great form and the body of skillful means—this is the Tathāgata.
Having spoken this verse, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is this an illusion?
The Buddha told the Great King:
“This is the Transformation Mother; as the Transformation Mother has taught, so too is the practice of the Bodhisattva.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla’s teacher, Maṇibhadra, ascended into the air to the height of seven tala trees and spoke these verses:
“Just as a jackal Constantly roams with a lion,”
Though we have long been accustomed to one another, our voices are not of a kind;
hearing his voice, I would die of terror—how much less could I roar like a lion?
I am like that small beast; though I have long been his teacher, I am no match for him.
Unable to endure the roar of the Hero among Men, his voice of fearlessness,
if this were not a skillful means, I would surely have died.
Like a jackal, how could I possibly receive such offerings?
I practiced the ways of ignorance, which Bodhisattvas have entirely abandoned;
toward all sentient beings, they regard them as equal to an only child.
The Buddha manifests immeasurable illusions that sentient beings are unable to comprehend.
Though he may manifest as hundreds of thousands of billions of Brahmin teachers, sentient beings do not know it;
only a Buddha knows the Buddha’s illusion.
One should know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the sovereign king among all illusions.
At that time, the wife of the teacher Maṇibhadra spoke these verses:
"Alas, all sentient beings, Not knowing the Buddha’s merit,
Claimed her to be the real Ciñcā-mānavikā, Failing to recognize her as a transformation of the Tathāgata."
He manifests himself in my form; such is the nature of his illusory transformations.
Great King, you should know that the Buddha’s body is inconceivable;
even those outcaste *caṇḍālas* would not dare to approach the King.
Constantly terrified and fearing death, how much more so when confronted with speech?
Thinking, "This person is a human, and I am also a human," they do not dare to associate with one another;
how much less could gods and humans draw near to them and transform their minds toward the Buddha?
Immeasurable devas, nāgas, and spirits constantly make offerings to the Tathāgata;
as for those who harbor evil intentions toward the Buddha, their lives are immediately cut short.
Through skillful means, the Buddha manifests various kinds of illusions.
He restrains future sentient beings from immeasurable unrighteousness;
the Buddha’s illusion is the Great Illusion, the Tathāgata’s body of skillful means.
Having spoken these words, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard of and witnessed such rare and extraordinary events, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness as he addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Is this an illusion?”
The Buddha said,
"Great King! That teacher, his wife, and Aṅgulimāla’s mother— those three persons are all my own illusions."
"I manifest inconceivable illusory transformations; it is because I have taught and transformed Aṅgulimāla that I deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I shall practice great giving for seven days; Aṅgulimāla Tathāgata is currently present as a field of merit.
The Buddha said to the king, "So it is, so it is."
At that time, the devas, nāgas, and spirits together spoke these verses:
"Homage to the King of Illusory Transformation, Who is fully endowed with great vigor;
The Tathāgata’s body of skillful means, Perfectly complete in the marks of skillful means."
Through skillful means, he enters parinirvāṇa and manifests the relinquishing of his relics.
The Tathāgata’s body is boundless, and his wisdom is likewise boundless;
his excellent reputation is boundless, and his power of light is boundless.
The Tathāgata’s body is boundless; the Secret Keeper is without limit.
His speech is also boundless, and his concealment is likewise without limit.
Boundlessly he illuminates the world, and his radiance is also boundless.
His merit exceeds all measure; it is beyond praise and immeasurable.
With unimpeded wisdom like space, the Tathāgata is the body of space.
He brings comfort to Mañjuśrī and to those such as us.
It is for the sake of Aṅgulimāla that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has come.
Whether he comes or does not come is not something we can know;
the Tathāgata regards all beings as he does Rāhula.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the assembly of devas, nāgas, spirits, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and King Prasenajit all admired the conduct of Aṅgulimāla and the conduct of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. They vowed to be born in that land, and all gave rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, leaping for joy with great delight.
